Eckert's fut
items.text:
Southampton give head coach Eckert new deal
- Published
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has signed a new contract at the Championship club until 2029.
The 33-year-old German's existing deal was expiring at the end of this season after being handed the role permanently last December.
Eckert's future was thrown into doubt over the summer, having been at the centre of an investigation by the Football Association over his role in the 'Spygate' scandal.
He could have been handed a lengthy suspension that would have threatened his job, but was ultimately given a suspended six-week ban and £28,000 fine.
"I'm very happy we have come to the point that we can make it official now," Eckert told the club website., external
"We've had some conversations that started a couple of weeks ago, and the goal was always clear: to show the same commitment we have had for the last 12 months.
"There is a lot that has happened in the last 12 months but the commitment from the club, from [owner] Dragan (Solak), [technical director] Johannes (Spors) and [chief executive] Phil (Parsons), and the supporters, means everything to me.
"I am very grateful for that. We have started a journey that is not even halfway through - there is a lot more to come."
Last season, Eckert, after taking over from the sacked Will Still, led the Saints from 21st in the table to a fourth-placed finish, also reaching the FA Cup semi-final where they took the lead before being beaten by Manchester City.
They were set to face Hull City in the play-off final but were thrown out after admitting spying on three clubs including Middlesbrough before the semi-final.
Saints were also deducted four points before the start of this campaign - if not for that penalty, they would be fourth in the table and one point off the leaders.
Regardless, they have started the campaign well and sit seventh after 15 matches, five points off the automatic promotion places.
Despite last season's controversy, Eckert has been boisterously backed by the Southampton fans at home matches this season.
He signs his new deal exactly a week from before Southampton face Middlesbrough for the first time since the Spygate saga unravelled.
"I think it's a great commitment from both sides; from the club to Tonda, and from Tonda to the club," sporting director Johannes Spors added.
"I'm very happy we have achieved this agreement before the end of the international window, allowing us to go into the busy schedule that is ahead of us with clarity.
"Tonda is very talented and very precise with a great analytical brain, but also has the personality and authority that you need, even at a young age. It is very clear this is the right place for him, and I'm very happy that he feels that too."
Eckert 'highly regarded internally and externally'
BBC Radio Solent's Southampton commentator Adam Blackmore:
This is good news for all parties, but especially for Saints and their players.
Tonda Eckert has effectively signed a new two-and-a-half-year contract, which while not a long deal, gives the club some protection from any admirers who come calling in the future, and gives the players some stability and reassurance.
At 33, Eckert is a coach who, despite the spying scandal of this year, is highly regarded internally and externally.
He and Johannes Spors seem to be building something at Southampton.
He's accrued 96 points from 48 Championship games, pretty remarkable stuff for a first-time head coach, and now Saints' best chance of keeping him until the end of this new deal is if they get promotion this season.
If Eckert can get them up, I already have confidence he can guide them to first-season safety if the club can keep him.

items.title: Uganda restricts cross-border movement, public gatherings amid Ebola threat
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 20 – Uganda has imposed fresh restrictions on public gatherings and cross-border travel in 34 high-risk districts bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) as authorities intensify efforts to prevent another Ebola outbreak.
The measures include a ban on concerts, festivals
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 20 – Uganda has imposed fresh restrictions on public gatherings and cross-border travel in 34 high-risk districts bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) as authorities intensify efforts to prevent another Ebola outbreak.
The measures include a ban on concerts, festivals and political rallies without clearance from the Ministry of Health, alongside mandatory 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation for Ugandans returning from the DRC.
The government has also tightened passenger screening at airports, introduced stricter monitoring of hotels and schools, and restricted the movement of humanitarian workers and bodies across its borders.
The restrictions, which took effect immediately, follow concerns over continued movement between Uganda and the DRC, including through unofficial crossing points that could facilitate the spread of the deadly virus.
In a public health advisory issued on November 19, Uganda’s Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Diana Atwine said the National Task Force on Epidemic Preparedness and Response had approved the additional interventions following an assessment of the risks posed by the outbreak in the neighbouring DRC.
“With the current heightened surveillance, the ministry has observed continued movement of people across our borders, including through ungazetted crossing points, which has increased the risk of the disease entering Uganda and spreading to our communities and to other countries,” Atwine said.
She emphasised that the new directives were additional safeguards, with previously announced restrictions remaining in force.
Under the new guidelines, authorities in the 34 designated border districts have been instructed to monitor new arrivals and people relocating into their communities. Local leaders, particularly Local Council chairpersons, must be notified immediately of new arrivals and movements into the affected areas.
Organisers of mass gatherings will also be required to obtain written authorisation from the Ministry of Health before holding concerts, festivals, political rallies or similar events in the designated districts.
The government has warned that individuals who illegally cross into the country, as well as those who facilitate unauthorised border movements, will face legal action.
Ugandans arriving from the DRC will undergo mandatory health risk assessments before being placed under 21-day quarantine or monitored self-isolation.
The restrictions also extend to humanitarian operations, with aid workers required to obtain clearance from the Director General of Health Services before undertaking cross-border movements.
The transportation of bodies into or out of Uganda will similarly require prior government authorisation.
At Entebbe International Airport, authorities have introduced enhanced screening and infection prevention measures for both arriving and departing passengers.
Travellers will be required to complete passenger locator forms before boarding to facilitate contact tracing, while airlines and other transport operators risk sanctions if they knowingly transport passengers without proper authorisation or documentation.
Uganda has also tightened controls in the education and hospitality sectors. Day scholars travelling between Uganda and the DRC in the designated border districts will no longer be permitted to cross under the new restrictions.
Boarding students who may have been exposed to the virus must undergo 21 days of quarantine in designated facilities before returning to school.
Hotels and other accommodation facilities have been directed to maintain accurate guest registers, verify visitors using valid identification documents and provide the records to health and security authorities when required.
Schools, hospitals, transport terminals, places of worship and other public facilities have also been instructed to provide handwashing facilities and strictly observe infection prevention and control measures.
To strengthen public awareness, radio stations operating in the affected border districts have been directed to dedicate at least two hours every month to Ebola prevention campaigns.
Kenya’s Ebola threat
Uganda’s heightened surveillance comes as Kenya approaches the end of its Ebola monitoring period following an outbreak linked to a traveller who passed through Uganda after arriving from the DRC.
Kenya confirmed its first case on October 6, involving a man who had travelled from the DRC through Kampala before arriving in Nairobi. The patient died on October 5, becoming the index case in the country’s outbreak.
Health authorities subsequently identified eight secondary infections, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to nine. All infections were linked to a single transmission cluster, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
The outbreak claimed two lives, including the index patient and his 65-year-old mother.
Kenya is now working towards a possible declaration of being Ebola-free around December 23, provided no new infections are detected.
The 42-day countdown began on November 12, following the discharge of the last patient and the completion of the mandatory 21-day monitoring period for the final contacts on November 11.
The 42-day period represents twice the virus’s maximum incubation period of 21 days and is the standard requirement for declaring an Ebola outbreak over.
Uganda’s latest restrictions also reflect its own experience with the disease earlier this year, when it recorded 20 confirmed cases between May and June 2026.
The infections comprised 15 imported cases from the DRC and five secondary infections among contacts, with two deaths reported.
Uganda declared its outbreak over on July 28, with the World Health Organisation following on August 27 after the country went 42 days without recording a new confirmed infection.
However, the continued movement of people across its border with the DRC has kept the threat of fresh infections alive.
By mid-November

items.title: FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?

items.text:
FIFA election 2027: Can Diallo or Tashima defeat Infantino?
November 20, 2026
Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 FIFA member nations cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.
Gianni Infantino – the powerful incumbent
Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under his leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.
During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia—a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.
At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.
Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate—whether it be his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia, or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly following the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.
A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.
Philippe Diallo – Europe's principled alternative
Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.
He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).
"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.
"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."
Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.
Kozo Tashima – an underdog as a possible king maker?
The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.
During a press conference in Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.
"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.
"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."
Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations – the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino – makes him a longshot to win the election.
But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.
"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," Tashima said.
"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.
However he also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.
If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

items.summary:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercise
items.text:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," he said.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland and in July a cruise missile also landed in Poland.

items.text:
Nations League quarterfinal draw: Spain face France, England play Norway
World Cup winners and European champions Spain have reached three of the four Nations League finals, winning in 2023.
World champions Spain will face France while England will play Norway in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League after the draw took place on Friday.
Spain beat France 2-0 in the semifinals of the World Cup in the United States in July on the way to winning the trophy. They also defeated Les Bleus 5-4 in the semifinals of the last edition of the Nations League last year.
The quarterfinals will be played over two legs in late March with Spain at home first after coming second in Group A3 while France topped Group A1.
Spain won the Nations League in 2023 while France beat them to win the 2021 final.
England topped Group A3 on goal difference after beating Spain away in their last outing, and their reward is a two-legged last-eight tie with Norway with the first leg on Norwegian soil.
England edged Norway in the World Cup quarterfinals this year before losing to Argentina in the semifinals.
The other quarterfinal ties will pit reigning Nations League champions Portugal against the Netherlands and Belgium against Germany.
The winners of the quarterfinals will advance to the final stages, which will be held in June at a venue yet to be decided.
Spain or France will play the Netherlands or Portugal in the single-leg semis, and England would face Belgium or Germany should they get past Norway.

items.title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
items.summary: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Si
items.text:
Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.
Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’
“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”
Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device filesystem.
Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.
“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

items.text:
Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
HUNTSVILLE, Texas — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.
And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.
The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.
Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.
Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"
Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."
Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."
After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.
The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.
Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.
She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state's procedures.
Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.
Asked if he was faking, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."
"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.
Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.
"David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right," she said Thursday. "Finally after 30 years, justice has been served."
Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.
Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."
Florida has now carried out more than half the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

items.text:
What does the ICJ’s Rohingya genocide ruling mean for Gaza?
The case sets a precedent for establishing a state’s intent to commit genocide beyond explicitly written orders.
After seven years of deliberations and investigations, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its minority Rohingya population.
Thursday’s ruling by the United Nations’ top court in The Hague has been viewed as historic, the first genocide verdict it has handed down since it was established in 1945.
For the majority-Muslim Rohingya – 1.2 million of whom are languishing in cramped refugee camps in Bangladesh while more than 500,000 remain trapped and targeted in Myanmar – it marked vindication and international recognition of their suffering following decades of persecution, torture and killings at the hands of the Myanmar military and non-Rohingya rebel groups in their home state of Rakhine.
This judgement has given hope to other persecuted populations around the world. It now sets a precedent to establish a government’s intent to commit genocide – a difficult aspect of such cases.
Experts say the verdict has strong implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza, which is one of those pending at the ICJ.
Just as Rohingya people celebrated and cried tears of joy when the court’s president pronounced a genocide ruling three hours into his readout of the verdict, many are wondering if this is a sign that Palestinians, too, will one day be able to do the same.
“This judgement will not decide the Gaza case,” Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, however, told Al Jazeera. “But it may determine the legal lens through which Gaza is eventually judged.”
Here’s what we know:
What is South Africa’s case against Israel?
On December 29, 2023, three months into Israel’s war on Gaza, South Africa filed an application against Israel at the Hague court, alleging that Israel was – and is – committing genocide against the Palestinian people living there.
Pretoria requested that the ICJ first approve emergency measures to protect civilians by immediately ordering Israel to suspend its military operations.
In two days of hearings in January 2024, the ICJ ruled that it is “plausible” that Israel’s actions could amount to genocide and ordered provisional measures requesting it “take all measures” to prevent the crime, despite Israel’s arguments that it was acting in self-defence following the deadly Hamas-led attacks on army outposts and villages in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people.
In March 2024, after South Africa had requested additional measures in light of Israel’s continued mass killings in Gaza, the court ordered Israel to ensure that food enters the enclave, finding that Palestinians in Gaza were facing famine and starvation.
In a third order in May that year, the ICJ ordered Israel to halt a deadly ground invasion in Rafah.
Israel did not comply with any of these orders, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have concluded.
At the time of the hearings in January 2024, some 23,000 people – including 10,000 children- had been killed in Gaza.
As of now, close to 75,000 people have been killed in Gaza, including an estimated 21,000 children. That does not include the thousands of people who are still missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
At least 1,662 people have been killed since an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire agreement was announced between Israel and Hamas.
A verdict on whether Israel is committing genocide is expected to take several years as the two parties must submit written arguments and counterarguments. South Africa’s next submission will be in November 2027.
How is the Gaza case similar to The Gambia’s Myanmar case?
For both the Rohingya and Palestinians in Gaza, legal proceedings have offered little immediate solace: tent camps are being washed away amid intense storms for both refugee communities. Civilians are also still being killed – by continuing Israeli strikes on Gaza, most recently on the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza, and by violence against Rohingya in Myanmar from both military and rebel groups.
The two cases have important legal parallels.
The Gambia accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya in November 2019.
That was two years after the Tatmadaw, Myanmar’s feared military, first began “clearance operations” that it claimed were a response to attacks on police posts by the rebel Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, which is fighting for Rohingya independence.
Myanmar denied committing crimes against civilians despite photos, videos and satellite images which showed mass killings and razed Rohingya villages, and despite gruelling accounts of torture and rape from thousands of survivors, as well as hate speech spread by senior Tatmadaw commanders.
On Thursday, nine of the ICJ’s 15-judge panel on the Rohingya case ruled that the “only reasonable inference” to be made from the evidence of widespread atrocities in Myanmar was that indeed, genocide had been committed.
The court said Myanmar had knowingly allowed civilian militias to participate in targeting Rohingya, failed to investigate or punish culpable commanders, acted with “intent” to destroy the group and prevent births, and violated provisional measures earlier issued in 2020 to preserve evidence.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
It ordered that Myanmar provide reparations and restitution by ensuring the safe return of Rohingya people to their lands, replacing damaged property and compensating those affected, accounting for missing people, reuniting families and ensuring dignified burials, providing med

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool magistrates court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abus
items.text:
A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the Manchester City forward withdrew his support for the prosecution.
Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool magistrates court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the Premier League match between Liverpool and Semenyo’s former club Bournemouth at Anfield on 15 August last year.
But Simon Jones, prosecuting, said: “Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him. In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case.”
District judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.
Semenyo, who left Bournemouth for Manchester City in January, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mogan was taken to hospital after a seizure.
The court had heard Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted racial abuse at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game. He was alleged to have said: “Hurry up and take the throw-in, you black bastard.”
Opening the case last month, Mr Jones said: “That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him. Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn’t believe what the male had said.”
Mogan then shouted: “I’m talking to you, you cunt,” the court heard. Witnesses also said they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.
Semenyo reported the incident to the referee and Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time. Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to “hurry up”.
Mogan declined to comment as he left court.

items.text:
US targets Iran’s ship-to-ship transfers: Can Tehran break the blockade?
CENTCOM declares vessels bypassing the Iran blockade could be stopped, boarded or even seized by US forces.
The United States military has tightened its naval blockade of Iran, warning that vessels receiving Iranian cargo through ship-to-ship transfers will face military action.
US Central Command (CENTCOM), in an advisory on Wednesday, said ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade”.
The move is aimed at closing a potential loophole that has allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets, despite Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports and oil exports since mid-July.
It comes as Tehran seeks ways to revive its oil exports, with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) repeatedly warning of retaliation against attacks on Iranian vessels.
Analysts say that while Iran is unlikely to break the blockade militarily, it could seek to make its enforcement politically and economically costly for Washington, raising the risk of a wider regional confrontation.
“This is potentially one of the most dangerous escalation scenarios we have seen in recent weeks,” Andreas Krieg, associate professor in Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
So, can Iran circumvent the blockade, and could attempts to do so trigger a wider confrontation?
What was the CENTCOM advisory?
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Wednesday that ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be evading the blockade.
“Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline,” CENTCOM said.
“Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated.”
CENTCOM also warned that ships failing to comply with its orders could face enforcement action, including the use of force.
Washington initially imposed the blockade on April 13, lifted it in June following an understanding with Tehran, and reinstated it on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.
What has Iran said?
Iranian authorities have yet to issue a direct response to CENTCOM’s announcement, but Tehran has repeatedly warned against US efforts to restrict its trade.
An article published by Iran’s semi-official state outlet Fars News Agency on Wednesday proposed sending a group of oil tankers through the blockade while threatening retaliation against regional energy infrastructure if US forces intervened.
“To break the naval blockade, Iran can move a group of oil tankers to break out of the blockade,” the commentary said.
It suggested that any attack or obstruction could prompt Iran to target energy infrastructure in the region, “especially UAE oil”.
Earlier this month, IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi rejected Washington’s ability to impose a comprehensive economic blockade on Iran.
“America can never achieve the type of economic blockade it’s after, whichever iteration it takes,” Mohebi said, according to Fars.
He also warned that Iran would retaliate if US forces attacked its vessels. “Naturally, in a war, they might hit one of our vessels. But we’ll hit harder,” he said.
Can Iran break the blockade?
Iran has managed to bypass parts of the blockade, but restoring large-scale crude exports presents a much greater challenge.
Before the US-Israeli war began in February, Iran exported roughly 1.5 million to 2 million barrels of crude oil per day, with China purchasing the vast majority of its shipments.
In October, Reuters news agency reported that at least eight tankers carrying Iranian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) had left the Gulf of Oman since July, citing shipping intelligence and security sources. Another vessel delivered jet fuel to Myanmar in September, it said.
On Thursday, Reuters, citing maritime monitoring service TankerTrackers.com, reported that a vessel was loading Iranian crude through a ship-to-ship transfer in the Gulf.
If the shipment reaches its destination, it could become the first successful crude export since Washington reinstated the blockade in July, it added. There was no confirmation from Iranian authorities on this development.
Nevertheless, academic Krieg says Iran lacks the military capabilities to challenge the blockade directly.
“Iran can circumvent parts of the blockade, but it cannot break it militarily in any sustainable way. The Americans possess overwhelming naval superiority,” he warned.
“However, policing every shipment, intermediary and ship-to-ship transfer is considerably more complicated than stopping tankers leaving Iranian ports.”
Krieg said Gulf-based commercial networks have also facilitated Iranian oil exports, including through ship-to-ship transfers, although the extent of official government involvement remains unclear.
Washington’s latest restrictions could therefore create tensions with Gulf partners whose commercial interests do not necessarily align with US sanctions policy.
“I think Iran’s objective would be less about physically defeating the blockade than making its enforcement politically and economically unsustainable,” Krieg said.
“Sending tankers to challenge American forces could be designed to create a confrontation rather than simply deliver oil. But commentary in Fars should not be mistaken for an authorised operational plan.”
What would it mean for the conflict and the bigger picture?
The tightened blockade raises the prospect of further military confrontation between Washington and Tehran, particularly if Iranian tankers attempt to defy US restrictions.

Government Funding Pressure On Iran War, National Security & Tech, Iowa Detonation
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.
- 🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.
Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.
- 🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China, partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.
The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.
- 🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week, prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust. Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.
Picture show
Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has reaffirmed the government’s commitment to protecting the independence of the Judiciary, saying a strong and effective justice system is critical to constitutional democracy, economic growth and social progress.
Kindiki said the administra
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has reaffirmed the government’s commitment to protecting the independence of the Judiciary, saying a strong and effective justice system is critical to constitutional democracy, economic growth and social progress.
Kindiki said the administration recognises the Judiciary’s central role in protecting fundamental rights, resolving disputes, upholding the rule of law and ensuring that government authority is exercised within constitutional limits.
“The Government recognizes that a strong, independent and effective Judiciary is indispensable to constitutional democracy, economic development and social progress,” he said.
Speaking on Friday in Nairobi during the launch of the State of the Judiciary and the Administration of Justice Annual Report for the 2025/2026 Financial Year, the Deputy President said the government’s commitment was reflected in increased budgetary allocations and institutional reforms since President William Ruto assumed office in 2022.
He disclosed that the Judiciary’s budget had increased to Sh30.4 billion in the 2026/2027 financial year, up from Sh27.15 billion in the previous financial year.
Kindiki said the government had also supported the appointment of an additional 53 judges to strengthen the courts’ capacity, address case backlogs and improve the efficiency of justice delivery.
The Deputy President further cited the enactment of the Judges’ Retirement Benefits Act, 2026, which he said addressed longstanding concerns over judges’ retirement welfare and strengthened the independence of the institution.
He noted that President Ruto had also acted on requests by the Judicial Service Commission, including improving judges’ retirement benefits and expediting the issuance of title deeds for court premises.
On Friday, Lands Cabinet Secretary Alice Wahome presented two title deeds covering the Supreme Court precincts and its parking area, ending years of uncertainty over ownership of the land housing the country’s highest court. She also handed over a title deed for a proposed court in Kapsabet town.
“I am glad that we have covered a lot of ground on the promises by the President, including presentation today of title deeds for Supreme Court precincts and the parking area,” Kindiki said.
The Deputy President also pointed to the Judiciary’s improved case clearance rate, noting that for the second consecutive financial year, courts had resolved more cases than were filed.
According to the report, the Judiciary disposed of 576,702 cases against 561,580 new filings during the period, translating to a case clearance rate of 103 per cent.
Of the cases resolved, 190,779 had been pending for more than one year, including 37,757 that had remained unresolved for more than five years.
However, Kindiki challenged the Judiciary to intensify efforts to clear the more than 341,000 cases that have been pending for over a year, warning that delays in the administration of justice undermine public confidence and economic activity.
“The Judiciary must continue playing its rightful role by reducing delays, strengthening commercial dispute resolution and ensuring that justice delivery supports economic and social progress,” he said.
He also announced progress in the implementation of the Judicial Performance Improvement Project Phase II, a Sh26 billion infrastructure programme approved by Cabinet in June in partnership with the World Bank.
The project targets the modernisation of the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal, consolidation of infrastructure for tribunals and Judiciary administration, as well as the establishment of a permanent home for the Kenya Judiciary Academy.
Kindiki said the investments would address infrastructure gaps, improve working conditions and strengthen the Judiciary’s institutional capacity.
He further assured that outstanding legislative proposals, including the Tribunals Bill and the Kenya Judiciary Academy Bill, as well as the review of the Small Claims Court Act, were being fast-tracked.
The Deputy President maintained that investment in the justice system should receive the same attention as infrastructure development, arguing that an efficient Judiciary provides the legal certainty needed to attract investment and support enterprise.
“Just as we invest in roads, energy and digital connectivity to support economic activity, we must invest in a justice system that provides legal certainty, protects rights and facilitates investment and enterprise,” he said.

Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
There is a certain thrill in spotting a dollar bill on the ground. It's free money! Well one lucky person found a Georgia O'Keeffe painting in her aunt's closet, under a pile of fur coats. The Smithsonian magazine reported the painting, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I," is part of a three-part series based on Keeffe's time in northern New Mexico. O'Keeffe has described her time there as particularly impactful.
The woman's aunt received the painting as a graduation gift from her parents way back when. They bought it for $3,800. That's the equivalent of $42,000 in today's dollars. This week, it sold at Christie's for $4,878,000 million. Double check your closet, people.
Coming up: 
- Why old software is so risky
- Why Steam is pulling in less revenue from NEW games
- What cohost Adrian Ma is reading this week
News We're Watching
This has been a long and strange week of outages from United Airlines to Apple Pay to the F.A.A. It's got many people thinking about this seemingly omnipresent threat of cyberattack. The agencies and companies experiencing the outages insist they're unrelated to cyberattacks. But there is a lot of concern right now about how vulnerable the U.S. is to these digital threats with the combination of fast-growing AI and decidedly fragile infrastructure.
Case in point, earlier this month, Europe faced ANOTHER hack on its supermarket refrigeration. Grocery stores and butcher shops across seven countries saw their fridges and freezers turned up to more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
It wasn't some complicated, sophisticated attack. It was hackers that found a vulnerability in old software. A vulnerability that had existed for a long time.
"That's where attackers see a big opportunity," said Aaron Mitchell, CEO of HeroDevs. "That's an easy way for me to get access and start to do some real damage."
After all, there is a lot of old software out there. Ones that touch utilities, hospitals, and critical infrastructure - or airlines. In some cases, companies didn't feel much urgency to address security gaps.
HeroDevs is a cybersecurity firm that does the addressing FOR companies. They help maintain support for a certain kind of software called open-source. When a software reaches end-of-life, and a company has moved on to new ideas, they might pay HeroDevs to maintain it and (importantly!!) patch vulnerabilities.
That could be more important than ever because AI is helping find a record number of these vulnerabilities. Last week, VulnCheck, a cybersecurity consulting firm, posted that more than 100,000 vulnerabilities have been found and disclosed so far this year, more than double than 2025. Hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities 33% faster compared to 2025.
In other words, vulnerabilities in outdated software are a prime target for hackers.
"About half of all exploits that happen, known exploits of a vulnerability, are happening on versions that are no longer supported by the maintainer," said Mitchell. "That number is rapidly growing."
This is a problem because countless websites, companies, and governments have outdated software somewhere.
Just last month, AI discovered two flaws in a programming language known as PHP that's built more than two-thirds of websites. The flaws could give a bad guy total access and even remote control of a web server without a password. An alert went out with a patch for every software to download.
"It was a huge deal, and for the whole week the whole internet was kind of on fire trying to get this thing patched," said Mitchell.
Still, in some cases, Mitchell said there were documented cases of websites that DID get exploited.
This is one example of how a small entrance for bad guys can be so dangerous. But these little doorways keep popping up. On Tuesday, an AI company revealed a critical vulnerability in Java known as Java4Shell prompting websites and companies to quickly take actions to patch against it.
As we can see and perhaps even feel, hackers are taking advantage. The most common cyberattack on utilities involves outdated software. Early this month, a cyberattack hit French blood banks, looking to increase temperatures using a similar tactic to the refrigeration hacks, although French authorities caught the attack in time and stopped it.
Richard Horne, the head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said that "vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long." In 2028, the UK predicts AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.
For now, Aaron Mitchell says, exploitation of vulnerabilities isn't taking off as much as it could be, "but every day that goes by, we get that much closer to the edge."
Just yesterday, Axios reported President Trump's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his role. He did not want to serve an additional two-year term, leaving an important role to be filled.
Today's Indicator
We got this economics podcast before GTA VI
If you HAVEN'T listened: This is the week of Grand Theft Auto VI. The wildly hyped game has already collected more than $1.5 billion in pre-sales. But the game itself is almost like a cover charge for an entire digital world, and, importantly, economy.
"Take-Two Interactive learned from GTA V that selling a product at retail is great, but better yet, what if you could continue to sell expansions and in-game events and items over a longer term?" said Joost van Dreunen, a professor at the NYU Stern School of Business.
GTA VI isn't launching its story mode with micro-transactions. That will likely come with the online mode of the game, expected to be released next year. The story mode can hook players into the world, and the online mode can keep them there. THEN you might start wanting to buy a few things.

items.text:
Newcastle United vs Arsenal: Premier League – Predictions, lineups, preview
As players return from international break, Premier League leaders Arsenal face Newcastle United away on match day 11.
Who: Newcastle United vs Arsenal
What: Premier League, match day 11
Where: St James’ Park, Newcastle, United Kingdom
When: Saturday, November 21, at 5:30pm (17:30 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 14:30 GMT before our live text commentary stream.
Club football returns this weekend following the international break, with Premier League leaders Arsenal looking to pick up where they left off in Saturday’s trip to Newcastle United.
The Gunners defeated Hull City 1-0 in their last league game before the break, extending their winning streak to five games after a promising start to their title defence.
The star-studded trio of Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard and Bukayo Saka have kept the red half of North London happy with their combined nine league goals. But Mikel Arteta’s side will once again have to do without their injured winger Saka for the upcoming test at St James’ Park.
Newcastle, on the other hand, come into this game on the back of a 1-1 draw with Fulham and eager to get back to winning ways.
Anthony Elanga, Harvey Barnes and Joe Willock have been the most prolific goalscorers for the Magpies, who are winless in three games.
How have Arsenal played this season?
Arsenal are the best performers in the Premier League this season.
After 10 games, the Gunners lead the table with 27 points, with nine wins and one defeat.
They have a five-point lead over second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion, and six points more than third-placed Manchester City.
How have Newcastle played this season?
Newcastle are in the bottom half of the table, sitting 12th with 12 points.
The Magpies have won three games, drawn three and lost four.
What happened when Arsenal and Newcastle last met?
The teams last met in the Premier League on April 25. Arsenal won 1-0 that day at the Emirates Stadium, thanks to a ninth-minute thunderbolt from Eberechi Eze.
Predictions: Newcastle vs Arsenal
Opta’s supercomputer has picked Arsenal as the favourites.
Arsenal are predicted to have a 56.4 percent chance of winning, while Newcastle’s odds of victory are 21.7 percent. There is a 21.9 percent probability of a draw on Saturday.
Form guide
(Last five Premier League matches; latest game first)
Newcastle: D-L-W-L-L
Arsenal: W-W-W-W-W
Head-to-head
(Only in the Premier League)
- Matches: 62
- Arsenal wins: 38
- Newcastle wins: 13
- Draws: 11
Team news and predicted lineups
Newcastle
Brazilian midfielder Joelinton, who has not featured since the start of this month, is doubtful with a knock, while full-back Tino Livramento is available.
“I don’t want to be too precise with the medical update. We will get feedback from the specialists and we will find out how long Joe will be out,” coach Matthias Jaissle said about Joelinton.
“We had nine injuries – now most of them are back; slowly but surely we will get them back to match fitness,” the manager added. “We need to be patient with them. It gives us flexibility.”
Predicted Newcastle XI:
Lukas Hornicek; Amar Dedic, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall; Sean Steur, Lewis Miley, Jacob Murphy, Yoane Wissa, Harvey Barnes; William Osula
Arsenal
Defender William Saliba is set to return from a long injury layoff that has kept him out since the 2026 World Cup semifinals in July.
But winger Saka is expected to remain out for another month with a thigh injury.
“We had another test,” said Arteta on Friday. “[Saka] is evolving really well but looks like it’s going to be an eight-week injury, more or less, so I think it’s four at the moment, so it’s a while for him to be back with the team.”
Midfielder Martin Zubimendi picked up a hamstring injury on international duty last week, and Arteta said he would be out for a “few weeks”, while youngster Max Dowman is serving a suspension.
Predicted Arsenal XI:
David Raya; Jurrien Timber, Ezri Konsa, Gabriel, Riccardo Calafiori, Bruno Guimaraes, Declan Rice; Noni Madueke, Martin Odegaard, Christos Tzolis; Kai Havertz

items.text:
San Francisco 49ers: Kyle Shanahan's side training at altitude in Colorado ahead of Minnesota Vikings clash in Mexico City
San Francisco 49ers are looking to extend their record to 8-1 with a victory against Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City on Monday; the team travelled to Colorado last Sunday and have been training at altitude this week: watch the game live on Sky Sports NFL
Friday 20 November 2026 12:24, UK
San Francisco 49ers are preparing for their upcoming clash against Minnesota Vikings at Mexico City's Estadio Azteca by training 7,258 feet above sea level in Colorado.
The 87,523-capacity stadium is situated at an altitude of 7,349 feet, and Kyle Shanahan's side are hoping to gain every advantage to improve on their 8-1 record this season against the Vikings on Monday morning, live on Sky Sports NFL.
Their training facility in Santa Clara, California, is at sea level, and the 49ers travelled to the Air Force Academy in Colorado on Sunday, following their 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys.
- Who is NFL MVP favourite? 'He is head and shoulders above'
- Latest NFL fixtures, results and UK kick-off times
- Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Kevin O'Connell's Vikings chose to practise in Minnesota rather than try to adjust to the altitude ahead of time.
The 49ers have historically altered their schedule to account for where games are played. They previously trained at the Air Force Academy four years ago in preparation for a game against Arizona Cardinals in Mexico City.
"One thing I know about our organisation that I really respect is everybody, from the top down, they'll do anything to try to help us get acclimated to whatever adversities or things that we have to face throughout the week," said running back Christian McCaffrey, who went to high school in Highlands Ranch, Colorado, 41 miles north of the Air Force Academy.
"So if we're going to play at altitude, coming here and getting acclimated is part of that. So I appreciate it."
Prior to week one, the 49ers spent a week in Melbourne, Australia, before their season curtain-raiser against Los Angeles Rams, who flew in shortly before the game.
San Francisco beat the Rams 27-7, looking sharper after adjusting to the 19-hour time difference.
"I think it's been nice to be here at practice and get some workouts in, and even just doing meetings and just living here for a week," quarterback Brock Purdy said.
"It's been a real thing that we've had to adjust to, and I'm glad that we're here. I think it's the right move for sure."
A half-speed training session was held on Wednesday, with Raheem Morris walking to the lectern on Thursday as if he was labouring to breathe the Colorado air.
"I'm out of breath right now," San Francisco's defensive coordinator said.
"You won't see the effect obviously into the game, but definitely good to get out here and get used to it."
Evans and Greenlaw back in training
Wide receiver Mike Evans (Achilles tendinitis) and linebacker Dre Greenlaw (neck) returned to practice on Thursday after sitting out Wednesday.
It was Evans' first practice since he left an October 19 win over Washington. He has missed the last three games.
"I thought he looked great," Purdy said. "He looked just like good old Mike from what I've been throwing him all year.
"Obviously, for me, I'm extremely encouraged by it. I'm going to go back, watch the film, see how it all looked. But just my initial thoughts were he looked great out there."
Evans was doing work on the side at the start of Thursday's session and then took part in drills with the receiving corps. Cornerbacks Renardo Green (back) and Upton Stout (shoulder), safeties Ji'Ayir Brown (ankle) and Siran Neal (foot) and defensive end Khalid Kareem (ankle) took part in the open portion of practice.
The only player not in uniform was back-up quarterback Mac Jones, who sat out with an illness.
Can the 49ers beat the Vikings in Mexico City? Watch the game from 1.10am (UK and Ireland time) on Monday, live on Sky Sports NFL and Sky Sports Main Event. Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract

Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says

- At least 8 people were killed and sev
items.text:
Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Zelenskyy said the Russian attack included 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles
- At least 8 people were killed and several bridges and energy facilities were hit
- Poland said it's airspace was violated during the Russian attack
Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:
Ukraine says dozens of Russian oil and defense targets hit in past 50 days
The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said that his forces had hit 40 Russian oil facilities and defense industry targets in the past 50 days.
Brovdi said via the Telegram that among those targets, five of them had been hit more than once.
He went on to say that the Dorogobuzh chemical plant in Russia's Smolensk region was struck on November 10 and November 20.
Ukraine has managed to adapt on the battlefield with the use of drone technology which has allowed hundreds of drone sorties, in some cases deep inside Russian territory, on a daily basis.
Zelenskyy says overnight Russian attacks 'one of the largest'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was targeted by more than 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, 27 of which he said were ballistic missiles.
"The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives," Zelenskyy said in a detailed post on social media platform X.
Zelenskyy listed what had been hit during the overnight strikes
- Energy facilities, substations and power lines, which Zelenskyy said nuclear facilities depended on
- Logistics and bridges across the Dnipro, three were reportedly struck
- Regular residential buildings damaged
- Zelenskyy says Russians used missiles with cluster warheads and described it as "one of the largest attacks"
He accused Russia of carrying out second strikes on targets that had already been hit, in so-called "double-tap strikes."
"People had essentially already been killed by the time specialists were inspecting the initial damage to the facilities, as the Russians were carrying out double-tap strikes," Zelenskyy said.
Most Russian missiles reportedly intercepted
Zelenskyy said that in all 79 cruise missiles had been intercepted and that fighter jets had been scrambled to deal with the aerial threats involving F-16s, Mirages and MiGs.
"Ballistic missiles are, unfortunately, much more difficult to deal with, and that depends not on our capabilities but on the supply of missiles by our partners," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's leader called for a "clear response" from the global community.
It is important that our partners not only issue statements in support of Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also follow through on specific agreements on air defense," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed out the timing of the latest attacks and said Putin launched them "in a highly demonstrative manner – following weak meetings in China."
"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror, precisely these attacks on life," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine death toll rises to 8 after Russian bombardment
Ukrainian officials said that the death toll has risen to at least 8 following an overnight Russian aerial bombardment.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said six of the eight people killed were in Kyiv. Two deaths were also reported at a railway station in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 84 cruise missiles in the attack, adding that almost all of them were destroyed.
An unspecified number of ballistic missiles and more than 400 attack drones were also reported to have been destroyed.
Poland's defense chief confirms Russian attack on Ukraine 'impacted' Poland
Poland's Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said that several Russian flying objects entered Polish airspace during recent air attacks on Ukraine.
"Russian long-range aviation was operating, launching both Kinzhal and Kh-101 missiles, as well as a large number of jet-powered drones and conventional drones. … This Russian Federation attack on Ukrainian territory, which also had an impact on the Republic of Poland, was one of the largest since the beginning of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine," the Defense Ministry quoted Kosiniak-Kamysz as saying.
It comes after Polish prosecutors reported earlier that a flying object had crashed in Poland's eastern Lublin region.
Polish officials said it had taken place during heavy Russian airstrikes on neighbouring Ukraine.
In July, a missile entered Polish airspace and crashed in the same region near the village of Tarnawa Kolonia.
According to the Polish government, it was a Russian CH-101 cruise missile.
Poland probing 'violations' of airspace at three locations
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that investigations were taking place at three sites after reporting that Polish airspace had been violated.
"In connection with violations of Polish airspace, authorities are conducting operations at three locations: Rudnik nad Sanem, Molodycz and Nowy Lipowiec (Lublin Province)," he said in a post on social media platform X.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he had convened a meeting of senior government and military officials along with the heads of security services in a post on X. He said there was currently no danger from the air.

In war-torn Ukraine, premature babies remain at risk during air raids, while young architects work to save a forgotten gem in Romania.
Deaths and damage reported in Russian missile strikes on Kyiv
Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that a Russian missile bombardment in Kyiv has killed at least three people and injured 13 others.
