In Oil and Gas operations, spudding is the first step in drilling a well and marks th
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Kenya’s countdown to producing crude oil from its South Lokichar sub-basin oil fields has begun in earnest, following the official spudding of the Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ Amosing 1 well pad.
In Oil and Gas operations, spudding is the first step in drilling a well and marks the official start of operations.
Following the recent rigging, levelling and commissioning of GW70, an onshore drilling rig leased from Great Wall Drilling Company (GWDC) at the Amosing 1&2 Oil Fields in Turkana County, the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum Cabinet Secretary Opiyo Wandayi presided over the spudding ceremony, effectively kicking off the first phase of the Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ US$ 6 billion drilling and crude oil production efforts.
Speaking at the spudding ceremony, CS Wandayi, flanked by Ministry of Roads and Transport Cabinet Secretary Davis Chirchir and Ministry of East African Community (EAC) Beatrice Askul among other government officials, confirmed that Kenya’s oil fields development efforts are running on schedule, with 1st December set as the official first oil production day.
On his part, CS Chirchir confirmed that the government is investing more than KShs 24 billion in the development of quality infrastructure projects such as roads in the oil fields region. The development of such infrastructure, he noted will elevate the regions social economic standing.
Describing Kenya’s first oil production agenda as a historical milestone, CS Wandayi said the government is supporting efforts to accelerate development of the oil fields in Blocks T6 and T7, as per the parliamentary-ratified Field Development Plan (FDP).
CS Wandayi stated that in the first phase, as set out in the FDP, Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ is expected to focus development on the Ngamia, Amosing, Twiga and Ekales fields, together referred to as NEAT, to produce more than 20,000 barrels per day. The six discoveries have a best-estimate recovery of 326 million stock-tank barrels over a 25-year contract period.
“This spudding event by the Government of Kenya’s contractor, Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ, marks a historical milestone ahead of first oil production,” CS Opiyo said. He added, “I am impressed by the sense of professionalism and patriotism of Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ and its contractors who are working flat out to meet targets set out in the Field Development Plan.”
The spudding and scheduled first oil production effectively marks Kenya’s entry into commercial crude oil production and is the culmination of the development programme in Turkana County. Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ will operate the project oil fields under Production Sharing Contracts (PSCs) with the National Government, under the oversight of the State Department of Petroleum and the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA).
Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ Managing Director Paul Limoh, while confirming the firm’s system readiness, said the first phase of 20,000 barrels per day production will be transported by road to Mombasa for stockpiling at the Kenya Petroleum Refineries Limited tank farms from 1st December. Beyond the first phase, the company plans to increase production to 50,000 bpd in the project’s second phase,
“At Gulf Energy, we are maintaining a tight delivery and project management schedule with the support of all our stakeholders, with a pledge to deliver against the FDP to world-class standards,” Limoh said. He added, “Overall, we are targeting six discoveries within Blocks T6 and T7. And the six discoveries have a best-estimate recovery of 326 million stock-tank barrels over a 25-year contract period.”
For this first phase, Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ has contracted Baker Hughes, a leading global Oilfield Services and Equipment (OFSE) solutions provider, to deliver Integrated Well Services. The firm has also engaged SLB, a leading energy technology and services company, to deliver the Early Production Facility (EPF).
Kenya’s crude oil is low in sulphur, asphaltene, and aromatics but moderately high in wax content, with a high wax appearance temperature (WAT) and pour point above ambient conditions. The associated gas is rich and sweet with some localised high carbon dioxide content. The crude oil is expected to be an intermediate, paraffinic, sweet oil with an API gravity of 30.5⁰ and will be indexed to Dated Brent.
Overall, Kenya stands to gain significant fiscal and economic benefits from the South Lokichar Basin oil fields development, which will position the country as a major East African oil producer. The Government of Kenya projects potential lifetime earnings of more than USD 2.9 billion (KES 371 billion), depending on prevailing global oil prices and production volumes over the life of the project.

items.title: Stoke and Birmingham proving you shouldn't judge a book by its cover
items.summary:
Stoke & Blues proving never judge book by its cover
- Published
Stoke City v Birmingham City: Third v first in the Championship.
That is a "tale of two cities" that did not look too likely to get written when Mark Robins' Potters started this season with three straight defeats and Blues won only two
items.text:
Stoke & Blues proving never judge book by its cover
- Published
Stoke City v Birmingham City: Third v first in the Championship.
That is a "tale of two cities" that did not look too likely to get written when Mark Robins' Potters started this season with three straight defeats and Blues won only two of their first eight league games under Chris Davies.
But, just like you should never judge a book by its cover, the footballing equivalent is to never judge any league table until after 10 games.
The season is now three months old - after Saturday's meeting at the Bet365 Stadium it will be more than a third of the way in.
And a clearer picture is starting to emerge as to whether what was once the "worst of times", especially in Stoke's case, might yet become the "best of times" before this 46-game campaign ends.
With 15 games gone, there are three clubs right at the top all on 29 points in what is already looking a ridiculously tight Championship table.
And two of them meet head on in front of an expected full house in the Potteries, having both been bang in form going into the latest international break.
Stoke are on a run of nine wins and only one defeat in 12 league games since the start of September, while Blues have won six out of seven since football returned after the first autumn international break.
So, how will things start to shape up after the second such break?
- EFL preview: Evans' gripes & unexpected departures 
  - Published3 hours ago
'One of most physical XIs in league' - Davies on Stoke
Stoke had the edge last season, winning 1-0 at home in September before drawing 1-1 in the return at St Andrew's in January, prior to Blues going into their late-season decline - and Davies can see the difference in the Potters.
"I watched the game back from when we played them a year ago and it looks very different," the Blues boss told BBC Radio WM.
"He [Mark Robins] has made a big impact from where they were last season. A real stamp of his identity.
"They've gone to a back five and, since then, they've conceded the fewest goals in the league - nine in 12 games.
"They've looked strong, particularly in the central areas. They've got bigger. They're now one of the most physical starting XIs in the league."
While extolling the Potters' defensive qualities, Davies is also well aware they have an attacking threat and he is an admirer of Stoke's American winger Jack McGlynn, who is their top scorer with five goals.
"I already knew a little bit about the boy McGlynn," said Davies. "He's been exceptional with the goals he's got.
"They're a team much like ourselves. I want us to go there as a measure to see how far we've come, if we can display what we've been showing recently."
'They've got some real talent' - Robins on Blues
Stoke boss Mark Robins' main concern is determining the fitness of his international contingent, having had 10 out of his 20-man matchday squad from their 2-1 win at Portsmouth away for almost a fortnight.
Of the 14 players involved that day, Swedish keeper Viktor Johansson, Bosun Lawal (Ireland), Robert Bozenik (Slovenia), Luke Graham (Scotland) and euphoric Northern Ireland pair Ethan Galbraith and Justin Devenny all played, while McGlynn was part of new Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino's USA send-off.
But now focus turns to Birmingham.
"They've changed a little bit," Robins told BBC Midlands Today. "They've clearly taken a lot from the Championship last season.
"They've got some players in form and some coming back from international duty, although less than we have.
"A lot [of their players] have been together a few seasons now - and they've got some real talent. But it gives us a chance to pit ourselves against the team at the top. The last time we did that was against Charlton."
Having already seen off one table-topping team in the Potteries this season, Robins is not getting carried away though.
"It's nice to be where we are," he added. "We've never been in the conversation before and we want to be in that conversation."
Stoke will hold a minute's applause before the game to mark the recent passings of Potters legend Peter Dobing and former manager Gudjon Thordarson.
'Blues taking risks, Stoke resilient' - old boy Clarkson
One local celebrity fan looking forward to Saturday's game more than most is a man with a foot in both camps - ex-Birmingham and Stoke full-back Ian Clarkson.
Boyhood Blues fan Clarkson made 174 appearances for the club between 1988 and 1993, when he moved on to Stoke, where he made a further 95 appearances.
After seeing out his career with Northampton Town, Kidderminster Harriers and Nuneaton Borough, Clarkson, now 55, then took his talents into the press box, reporting on Blues first for the Express & Star then the Birmingham Post - and he now coaches football in his teaching role at Repton College.
He has seen plenty of both clubs this season - and both have taken him slightly by surprise.
"Blues are a lot more inclined to attack than they were last season, they look more likely to take a few risks," Clarkson told BBC Sport.
"The signing of August Priske in January is obviously starting to reap rewards and it's bringing the best out of Jay Stansfield. Plus you've got good contributions coming from their wingers and two more on the bench to come on.
"Blues are playing some lovely football right now. Chris Davies is obviously a manager who works very hard at it. And they just seem to have got it right. They've clicked."
"Stoke are starting to look more like a Stoke City team, in the nicest possible way.
"Mark Robins is just one of those managers who, wherever he is, just seems to get better. The longer he stays at a club the better he gets. And they really do look far more resilient.
"There's something about the place that just feels different this season. They've got the fans back on side and that's more important than anything. Everyone knows how tough a place Stoke can be when it's bouncing."
As to who will win on Saturday? And where

items.title: China’s Shenzhen Summit Offers Hope for a More Peaceful World
items.summary: When Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to Shenzhen for a historic trilateral summit, the significance extended beyond the presence of three powerful leaders. It was also an opportunity to reaffirm a message the world urgently needs t
items.text:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to Shenzhen for a historic trilateral summit, the significance extended beyond the presence of three powerful leaders. It was also an opportunity to reaffirm a message the world urgently needs to hear: peace is precious, dialogue matters, and major powers have a responsibility to work together.
The historic meeting and the Declaration toward Peace that followed offered a reminder that diplomacy is most valuable when relationships are difficult. China, Russia and the United States have competing interests and different political systems. Yet their shared responsibility to safeguard peace should bring them into communication, not push them further apart.
For ordinary people, international stability is not an abstract concept. It is reflected in the price of fuel, the cost of food, the security of jobs, the confidence of businesses and the prospects young people have for their future. When tensions among major powers disrupt energy markets, trade routes or supply chains, households and communities thousands of kilometres away can feel the consequences.
The Shenzhen meeting therefore matters to people who may never follow diplomatic communiqués. A more stable relationship among major powers can help create conditions in which economies trade, businesses invest and countries focus on development rather than uncertainty.
China’s hosting of the summit placed this human dimension of diplomacy in view. Xi described the meeting as positive, constructive and fruitful, and urged the three countries to follow through on their consensus, strengthen communication and promote peace through cooperation. The emphasis was not simply on the leaders’ encounter, but on what sustained engagement could mean for the wider world.
The declaration reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. It also committed the three countries to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation. These words carry particular weight because the consequences of a nuclear conflict would be catastrophic for humanity, without regard to borders, wealth or political allegiance.
In an age when technology, military capability and geopolitical competition are advancing rapidly, keeping channels of communication open is essential. Dialogue can help reduce miscalculation, clarify intentions and create space for decisions that protect lives. It is not a guarantee of agreement, but it is a necessary safeguard against escalation.
The summit also addressed practical issues that touch people’s lives, including energy security and the stability of supply. The declaration set out plans to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products and reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows. For developing economies, predictable energy markets matter to transport, manufacturing, agriculture and the everyday cost of living.
China has consistently advocated cooperation rather than decoupling and disruption. Xi’s call to combine the countries’ strengths in resources, manufacturing and consumption to expand the benefits of cooperation reflects an approach that sees economic interdependence as an opportunity. When trade and supply chains function reliably, businesses can plan, workers can earn and consumers can benefit.
The discussion of United Nations reform is equally important. As permanent members of the Security Council, China, Russia and the United States acknowledged the need for the UN to respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its central mission of maintaining international peace and security. For Africa and other developing regions, a more responsive multilateral system is essential to ensuring that global decisions reflect a wider range of voices and realities.
China’s advocacy for a more representative international order resonates across Africa, where countries seek greater participation in decisions on finance, trade, security and development. African states should be able to engage international partners on the basis of their own priorities, building relationships that support industrialisation, infrastructure, technology, skills and opportunity.
Kenya, for example, depends on international trade, investment, affordable energy and stable markets. It has a practical interest in a world where major powers manage their differences responsibly and where cooperation remains possible across political divides. Peaceful coexistence is therefore not merely a diplomatic ideal; it is part of the environment that allows countries such as Kenya to pursue development.
The Shenzhen summit also reinforces an important principle: countries do not have to abandon their interests to cooperate. Xi has urged China and the United States to make the list of areas for cooperation longer and the list of problems shorter, while managing differences constructively. This recognises that disagreements may persist, but need not define the entire relationship.
The real test will be what happens after the meeting. Declarations acquire meaning through follow-up, regular communication and practical action. The summit cannot resolve every dispute, nor should its importance be measured only by immediate breakthroughs. Its value may lie in keeping dialogue alive and establishing habits of engagement at a moment when the world needs stability.
China’s message from Shenzhen is ultimately a human one. Behind every discussion of strategic stability are families hoping for security, young people seeking opportunity, farmers and businesses needing dependable markets, and communities that want resources spent on conflict to be directed towards better lives.
The world’s major powers will continue to compete. But competition need not close the door to cooperation. By bringing leaders together and calling for peaceful coexistence, mutual respect and dialogue, China has helped underline an enduring truth: the fu

items.text:
EU and UK hold a rare summit in bid to 'rebuild ties'
November 20, 2026
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham were set to announce deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first steps to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
What did Burnham say at the EU-UK summit?
Brussels said the agreements would only take effect if a deal is reached to lower university tuition fees for EU students studying in the UK.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
UK prime minister, who was greeted on arrival by a string quintet, said Britain should explore different options for its future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc.
On Monday, he said it was the "obvious truth" that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.
What is on the agenda?
Three key agreements were being discussed in Brussels: one to simplify food exports by reducing red tape, another to link the UK and EU emissions-trading systems, and a third to establish a "youth experience scheme."
It aims to facilitate British companies exporting food to Europe, as well as enabling young people to travel between the UK and EU for work and study without being subject to existing visa requirements.
A key obstacle was securing a commitment from the UK to reach a future agreement that would reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students. The EU made the implementation of the other agreements conditional on reaching such a deal.
The two sides had agreed on these initiatives shortly before the summit started, DPA news agency reported, citing EU diplomats and officials.
According to DPA, the agreements will only take effect if both sides reach a deal to lower tuition fees for EU students at British universities. They aim to reach an agreement on this issue within the next six months.
Speaking to AP news agency, a British government spokesperson said "the deal is done," adding that details would be published in a joint statement later.
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

Friday 20 November 2026 11:45, UK
England will take on Erling Haaland and Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals.
Thomas Tuchel's side finished top of their group thanks to their dramatic 3-2 win over Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium, while Norway finished second behind Portugal in Group D.
The two sides met in the 2026 World Cup quarter-finals, with a Jude Bellingham goal in extra-time sending the Three Lions through to the last four.
Should England progress, they will meet Belgium or Germany in the semi-finals. The other two quarter-final ties have seen world champions Spain drawn with France and Netherlands take on Portugal.
The quarter-finals will be two-leg ties and will take place in the March international break, with the first legs between March 25-27 and the second legs between March 28-30.
This will then be followed by the Nations League Finals, which will be held between June 9 and June 13, 2027.
The tournament will feature two semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final. The four semi-finalists will be invited to make bids to host the semi-finals and final.

items.title: James Bowen latest jockey to reveal death threat incident
items.summary:
James Bowen received death threat from disgruntled punter as jockey speaks out following similar Nico de Boinville incident
Bowen brothers were given security protection last year after a threat was made; fellow jockey Nico de Boinville revealed a similar incident earlier this week after threat made
items.text:
James Bowen received death threat from disgruntled punter as jockey speaks out following similar Nico de Boinville incident
Bowen brothers were given security protection last year after a threat was made; fellow jockey Nico de Boinville revealed a similar incident earlier this week after threat made to Nicky Henderson's yard. Warning: Readers may find some of the language in this story distressing
Friday 20 November 2026 12:24, UK
James Bowen has become the latest jockey to reveal he has been subjected to death threats from disgruntled punters, with the 25-year-old disclosing that he and champion jockey brother Sean required security protection following an incident last year.
Nico de Boinville was in the news earlier this week when a threat against his life had been phoned in to Nicky Henderson's yard following the defeat of an odds-on favourite at Plumpton.
That was far from the first incident of its kind, and Bowen, speaking in his DragonSports blog while he recovers from a broken wrist, said both he and his brother regularly receive abuse on social media - but one incident in particular stood out.
- Nicholls breaks record for Jumps wins with Warwick triumph
- Sober Glory storms to victory over Old Park Star on chase debut
He said: "Last season, at Ffos Las on October 16, 2025, we were both the subject of death threats during a race meeting, to the extent that we had security accompanying us between the paddock and weighing room for the next three or four days.
"It was something we kept largely to ourselves at the time, but recent events involving Nico de Boinville have brought the subject back into sharp focus.
"In our case, somebody made an anonymous telephone call, which I believe went to either the racecourse or the British Horseracing Authority, threatening to kill both me and Sean.
"It happened while we were both racing at Ffos Las. We were informed about it and, understandably, the authorities had to take it seriously.
"After our final race, we spoke to the police and explained everything we knew. There was security around us for the following few days, with people accompanying us to and from the paddock.
"Nothing much came of it afterwards, as far as I know, and we never heard anything further about who had made the call."
He went on: "You can perhaps understand why somebody might get frustrated if a horse they have backed gets beaten, but there is absolutely no justification for taking it to that sort of extreme.
"I hope the person who made the threat had no intention of carrying it out, but you cannot simply dismiss something like that.
"What is perhaps even more worrying is that receiving unpleasant messages has become such a regular occurrence that you almost become accustomed to it.
"I have had plenty of messages telling me they hope I break my legs or my neck. They tend to come through private messages on social media, particularly Instagram and X.
"It is not something that surprises me any more, which is probably quite sad when you think about it.
"You get hardened to a certain extent, and there is a bit of dark humour among jockeys about some of the things people send. Sometimes you have to laugh about it because otherwise you would cry."
If you have been affected by this story, support and guidance are available at sky.com/viewersupport

US appoints new cybersecurity chief after series of tech failures
Appointee Kirsten Davies says US has the chance to ‘dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come’.
The White House has fired the United States’s cybersecurity chief and appointed a replacement, days after widespread outages di
items.text:
US appoints new cybersecurity chief after series of tech failures
Appointee Kirsten Davies says US has the chance to ‘dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come’.
The White House has fired the United States’s cybersecurity chief and appointed a replacement, days after widespread outages disrupted air travel, banking and national security systems.
Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Department of Defense, was appointed on Thursday to replace Sean Cairncross, who was reportedly sacked.
President Donald Trump’s administration has come under scrutiny over its handling of outages that hit Microsoft, the air industry and banks.
A communications failure disrupted air traffic late last week, grounding all flights in the US for about four hours and causing more than 10,000 flights to be cancelled. The disruption is expected to have cost travellers more than $1.9bn in lost time and expenses, according to the Anderson Economic Group.
Microsoft has apologised after governments, businesses and individuals around the world were affected as server failures caused outages of email and websites.
This week, bank customers across the US reported problems accessing services after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.
The incidents have renewed questions about the vulnerabilities of critical infrastructure, most of which depends on modern-day technology.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies said in a social media post.
“Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernise and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future.”
US officials have said the outages were not caused by a cyberattack.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Wednesday that the disruptions were likely due to organisations using artificial intelligence to fix security flaws and carry out maintenance updates.

items.title: Gachagua threatens protests against IEBC over 2027 election
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 20 – Democracy for Citizens party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has warned President William Ruto and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) against manipulating the 2027 General Election.
Gachagua warned that Kenyans would not accept what he described as a rig
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 20 – Democracy for Citizens party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has warned President William Ruto and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) against manipulating the 2027 General Election.
Gachagua warned that Kenyans would not accept what he described as a rigged election, insisting that the IEBC must address opposition concerns over voter registration, identification cards and the announcement of presidential results before the country goes to the polls.
Speaking on Friday in Wamunyoro a day after a meeting between opposition leaders and IEBC officials, Gachagua claimed that there were worrying differences in how voters were being registered and identification cards issued in different parts of the country.
He alleged that voter registration was being conducted selectively in parts of the Rift Valley, claiming that some residents were receiving assistance to register while people in other regions faced delays.
“We want to know why you are having selective registration of voters in the Rift Valley. At Ruto’s place, votes are being registered, taken to homesteads. Why are you not doing the same in the rest of the country?” Gachagua posed.
He also questioned what he described as unequal access to national identity cards, alleging that some applicants in areas associated with the President were receiving the documents within days while others waited for up to 10 months.
Gachagua said the opposition had raised the concerns during its engagement with IEBC, arguing that unequal access to identification documents could affect the ability of eligible Kenyans to register as voters.
The DCP leader further questioned the time taken to process identity cards, claiming that applicants in some parts of the country waited between eight and 10 months, while others allegedly received them within three days.
Another issue raised by the opposition was the process of tallying and announcing presidential election results.
Gachagua argued that presidential results should be announced at the constituency level, insisting that the process should not depend on further tallying at the national level in Bomas of Kenya.
He maintained that the IEBC chairman’s role should largely be to add up results already declared at constituency level and announce the overall winner.
“The Constitution of Kenya says there shall be a presidential election in the 290 constituencies. The presidential election will be conducted at the constituency and will end there,” he said.
He questioned why presidential results should be taken to Bomas for further tallying, arguing that constituency returning officers should declare the results from their respective areas.
According to Gachagua, counting of presidential votes begins immediately after polling stations close, making it possible for constituency results to be established within hours.
The DCP leader also invoked the 2024 Gen Z protests, warning that Kenyans could mount fresh demonstrations if the electoral commission failed to address their concerns.
He said the protests witnessed during the Finance Bill demonstrations would be minor compared to what could happen if the 2027 election process was compromised.
“Don’t underestimate the resilience and the determination of the Kenyan people. That commotion you saw there during the Finance Bill is child’s play,” Gachagua warned.
He challenged the IEBC to engage political leaders and address the proposed electoral reforms, saying Kenyans were determined to protect the credibility of the next election.
“If you don’t want to engage the leaders, then Kenyans will engage you directly. And I can tell you, you cannot win any battle against the people of Kenya,” he said.
Gachagua maintained that the opposition wanted changes agreed upon before the election rather than waiting until disputes emerged after voting.

After a summit in Brussels on Friday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have co
items.text:
EU and UK seal reset deal
The European Union has struck agreements on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset deal has been sealed.
Downing Street said both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, and a link between their emissions trading systems. Details are due to be published in a joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations on topics ranging from student fees to manufacturing rules lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
More to come …

items.title: Lenku faces NCIC remedial action over remarks on Maasai political representation
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – The National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) has faulted Kajiado Governor Joseph Ole Lenku over remarks in which he described political parties that fail to give the Maasai community senior leadership positions as enemies, warning that the statements risked underm
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – The National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) has faulted Kajiado Governor Joseph Ole Lenku over remarks in which he described political parties that fail to give the Maasai community senior leadership positions as enemies, warning that the statements risked undermining peaceful coexistence.
In its Determination No. 5 of 2026, the commission found that Lenku’s remarks, made during a political gathering in Kajiado County on August 22, 2026, promoted political exclusion and threatened adverse consequences against individuals who chose alternative political paths.
The commission took issue with the governor’s use of the words “adui wetu” (our enemies) to describe political formations that did not accommodate Maasai interests in party leadership and nominations.
It also raised concerns over his warning that those who chose a different political direction would “utajipata taabani” (find yourself in difficulty), saying the language introduced an element of intimidation into political participation.
According to the commission, the remarks went beyond advocating for the political representation of the Maa community and risked alienating other communities living in Kajiado, which is home to people from diverse ethnic backgrounds.
“The remarks fell below the constitutional standard of responsible leadership and posed a risk to peaceful coexistence in Kajiado County,” the commission said.
The inquiry followed a video recording of the political forum in which Lenku addressed the place of the Maasai community in party leadership and nomination processes, particularly positions considered to belong to the Maa community in Kajiado and Narok counties.
Lenku appeared before the commission on September 17, 2026, accompanied by his lawyers and county officials, where he confirmed the factual accuracy of the remarks attributed to him.
However, through his lawyers, AMA Advocates LLP, the governor argued that his statements were made in his capacity as an elected leader and spokesperson for the Maa community, seeking to address historical injustices, land dispossession, marginalisation and political representation.
His legal team maintained that the remarks were directed at political parties and choices rather than ethnic communities, arguing that expressions such as “adui”, “hatuna uhusiano na wewe” and “taabani” referred to political association and electoral competition and did not amount to threats of violence, incitement or ethnic hatred.
The commission, however, rejected the argument that the political context placed the statements beyond its mandate, maintaining that political discourse must comply with constitutional standards on national cohesion and the rights of other citizens.
It said the governor’s position as an elected leader and influential political figure increased the potential impact of his statements, particularly their ability to mobilise supporters and deepen divisions.
The NCIC further acknowledged that demands for community representation, equitable political participation and redress for historical injustices were legitimate issues that could be raised in public debate.
However, it cautioned that such grievances could not justify language that intimidated people or portrayed those pursuing alternative political choices as enemies.
In its assessment, the commission cited Articles 27, 33(3) and 38 of the Constitution, which provide for equality and freedom from discrimination, responsible exercise of freedom of expression and the right to political participation.
Following its findings, the commission issued Lenku with a Notice of Remedial Conciliation proposing corrective, preventive and restorative measures aimed at addressing the concerns raised by his remarks.
The governor has been given seven days from the date of the determination to communicate in writing whether he accepts the proposed terms or wishes to suggest variations.
The commission clarified that its determination was administrative and conciliatory in nature and did not amount to a criminal conviction or a judicial finding of guilt. The proposed measures also do not carry criminal punishment.
It further emphasised that the findings do not restrict the Maasai community or any other group from advocating for political representation, addressing historical injustices or demanding equitable participation in public institutions.
Instead, the commission urged political leaders to pursue such demands through dialogue, democratic engagement and lawful political processes without threatening or excluding other communities.
The determination comes amid continuing political competition over community representation and party leadership in the Maa-dominated counties of Kajiado and Narok, where political alignments and nomination processes have remained sensitive issues.
The NCIC reiterated that political differences should not be allowed to undermine the rights, dignity and security of residents from different communities.

The United States has pitched a new plan to secure post-war Ukraine when it
items.text:
Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
NATO’s Article 5 says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all. Analysts say inclusion of Ukraine ‘stretches credulity’.
The United States has pitched a new plan to secure post-war Ukraine when its almost five-year war with Russia finally comes to an end.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner’s comments came just hours after an unprecedented summit involving Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. At that meeting, Putin promised to retaliate against Ukraine’s attacks on Russia.
Following the Berlin summit, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabokov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly stated that Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would trigger “a harsh response” from Russia.
So could NATO-like security guarantees really work for Kyiv in light of Russia’s opposition?
Here’s what we know:
What has Kushner said?
European countries have been angered by the European Union being largely sidelined in the stop-start US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi on Thursday has added to apprehension about whether the US president is serious about ending Russia’s war on Ukraine, particularly after his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his apparent recent overtures to Putin by relaxing sanctions on Russian oil.
But at a meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, a nearly 40-nation alliance of Ukraine’s European allies, in Berlin this week, Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff tried to reassure European leaders, telling them Trump had held discussions in Shenzhen on ending the war on Ukraine.
“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” Kushner said.
“We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war,” he added.
Kushner also said Russia is “comfortable” with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, which says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all.
“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but “obviously, it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.
Kushner said Trump also called in to the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin and the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week had produced no major breakthrough.
What is NATO’s Article 5?
Described as the “cornerstone” of the military alliance, NATO’s collective defence principle, contained in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, was developed in 1949 to create a mutual protective pact to counter risks posed by the Soviet Union at the onset of the Cold War.
According to NATO, committing to Article 5 means that each member of the alliance knows that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
That means that each NATO member is obligated to “take the actions it deems necessary to assist the ally attacked”.
When Article 5 is invoked, NATO allies are free to provide whatever form of aid and assistance is deemed “necessary to respond to the situation”.
However, it is not an automatic process. The article must be invoked and then agreed upon by NATO members and can take time to implement. First, there must be a meeting of the North Atlantic Council to assess whether the attack meets Article 5 criteria. Then there must be a unanimous political decision and declaration to invoke the article. This can be slowed down by deliberations, intelligence gathering and legal reviews.
After that, determining what is necessary to respond to a given situation is the individual obligation of each NATO ally and may not necessarily include military action. As NATO states: “It is therefore left to the judgement of each individual member country to determine how it will contribute.”
Each country consults with all other alliance members in terms of response and with the ultimate aim “to restore and maintain the security” of alliance members.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US by al-Qaeda.
The triggering of Article 5 saw “NATO engage actively in the fight against terrorism, launch its first operations outside the Euro-Atlantic area and begin a far-reaching transformation of its capabilities”, according to the alliance.
“By invoking Article 5, NATO members showed their solidarity toward the United States and condemned, in the strongest possible way, the terrorist attacks against the United States.”
What could ‘NATO-like’ security guarantees look like for Ukraine?
It is very unclear.
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided about offering Ukraine alliance membership during an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, such as Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic abo

items.title: World Toilet Day: Sanitation must become an affordable investment for every household
items.summary:
By Rose Muyanga,
Access to a safe toilet is fundamental to public health, dignity and well-being. While Kenya has made progress in expanding access to improved sanitation, disparities in household circumstances, infrastructure and affordability mean that more needs to be done to extend these gains t
items.text:
By Rose Muyanga,
Access to a safe toilet is fundamental to public health, dignity and well-being. While Kenya has made progress in expanding access to improved sanitation, disparities in household circumstances, infrastructure and affordability mean that more needs to be done to extend these gains to every community.
The 2025–2026 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey shows that 76 per cent of households have access to improved sanitation facilities. However, the proportion stands at 63 per cent in rural areas, compared with 93 per cent in urban areas. The survey also indicates that 45 per cent of the population has access to at least basic sanitation services, while 7.4 per cent still practise open defecation.
These findings underscore the importance of sustaining investments in sanitation while addressing the different needs of households. Access to an improved toilet is an important step, but safely managed sanitation also requires hygienic and durable facilities supported by appropriate waste containment and management systems.
The Ministry of Health’s Costed National Sanitation and Hygiene Roadmap 2023–2030 provides an indication of the investment required. It estimates that a basic G1 sanitation unit, designed to provide a clean and flyproof toilet, costs between KES 10,000 and KES 12,000 in hardware, depending on county conditions. A more durable individual G2 toilet with safe waste containment costs between KES 25,000 and KES 30,000.
The financial commitment also extends to maintaining good hygiene practices. The Roadmap estimates that basic household hand hygiene costs KES 7,048 annually, covering household promotion, handwashing facilities and soap. This highlights the need for sustained investment in sanitation infrastructure, reliable water access and everyday hygiene practices.
For households managing competing priorities such as food, rent and school fees, meeting these costs can require careful financial planning. Flexible financing arrangements can help spread the cost of improvements over time, enabling families to invest in better sanitation facilities while managing their other financial obligations.
This presents an opportunity for financial institutions to complement ongoing public efforts by developing accessible financing solutions that respond to household needs. These may include financing for durable, all-weather toilets, bathroom improvements, handwashing facilities and water connections.
For instance, KWFT’s Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) financing solutions support households to construct toilets, repair existing facilities and improve bathrooms and water connections. Through its Kisima Loan, the institution also finances water tanks for rainwater harvesting and storage, water purifiers, shallow wells, water pans and related equipment. Such financing can help families make gradual improvements to their living conditions while spreading the associated costs.
There is also scope to strengthen the role of women entrepreneurs in delivering essential water-related services. Women operating water-selling businesses, for example, can benefit from working capital to maintain stock and financing for equipment that improves efficiency and expands their services. Supporting these enterprises contributes to local service delivery while creating income-generating opportunities.
The benefits of improved sanitation are particularly significant for women and girls. Access to adequate household facilities can ease the responsibilities associated with water collection and sanitation management, while safe and private toilets in schools support menstrual hygiene, protect girls’ dignity and help reduce absenteeism. Improving sanitation therefore contributes not only to better health but also to women’s economic participation and girls’ educational opportunities.
These outcomes reinforce the connection between sanitation and broader development priorities, including Sustainable Development Goal 6 on clean water and sanitation, SDG 3 on good health and well-being, and SDG 5 on gender equality.
As we mark World Toilet Day, there is an opportunity to strengthen collaboration among government, financial institutions, development partners and the private sector to expand access to safe and affordable sanitation. Continued public investment in infrastructure, policy support and targeted interventions for vulnerable households can be complemented by private-sector financing and the provision of quality sanitation products and services.
Ultimately, improving sanitation requires sustained investment at both household and community levels. Making appropriate financing accessible can help more families take practical steps towards safer facilities, better hygiene and healthier living conditions, contributing to Kenya’s broader sanitation and development ambitions.
The author is the Managing Director, Kenya Women Microfinance Bank PLC.

items.text:
The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”
A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.
Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.
The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.
On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.
On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.
The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.
The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.
Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.
Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.
“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.
Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.
“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.
The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.
Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

items.title: Senate passes bipartisan energy bill amid environmental concerns
items.summary:
Senate passes bipartisan energy bill amid environmental concerns
As Americans struggle with rising energy costs and increased demand driven by artificial intelligence, the Senate on Thursday passed a bipartisan bill that will speed up the approval process for data centers and power plants.
The Bipar
items.text:
Senate passes bipartisan energy bill amid environmental concerns
As Americans struggle with rising energy costs and increased demand driven by artificial intelligence, the Senate on Thursday passed a bipartisan bill that will speed up the approval process for data centers and power plants.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, passed 62-33. Fourteen Democrats and one Independent joined most Republicans in supporting the bill. It now heads to the House. The bill was authored by two Democrats and two Republicans.
"Tonight, the passage of permitting reform in the Senate finally became reality and we took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people," said one of the bill's co-authors, West Virginia Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the bill would "cut through decades of red tape" and "save the average household hundreds of dollars each year, and Americans will see better roads, more American manufacturing, and better-paying jobs."
Rhode Island Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, who co-authored the bill, said "Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit."
Nationwide, the cost of a kilowatt-hour has risen faster than overall inflation: more than 6% in the last year and 39% in the last five years.
Whitehouse also said the bill would make data centers pay for the power they use. There has been considerable pushback by the public against data centers in the U.S., cutting across party lines.
Some climate change advocates say the U.S. needs to speed up building renewable energy projects and transmission lines and argue that the bill will allow the country to build more solar, wind and battery projects.
But major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have opposed the bill, arguing it will weaken environmental accountability.
Many Democrats have also opposed the bill. They say it will worsen pollution by making it easier to greenlight oil and gas projects and energy-hungry data centers, while weakening protections for clean air and water.
There is also concern the bill could undermine tribal rights.
"Don't sacrifice the Clean Water Act, hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty," said Washington Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell on X.
California Sen. Alex Padilla had similar concerns. "I support cutting red tape and getting more energy projects built, but not at the expense of tribal sovereignty and California's environment," he said.
Jeff Merkley, a Democratic senator from Oregon, called the bill "a bad deal."
"It opens the gates to a flood of natural gas for data centers while leaving expanded transmission of renewable energy subject to Trump's obstruction," he said on X.
In a recent social media post, President Trump urged Congress to approve the bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE."
Julia Simon contributed reporting to this story.

items.title: T20 the focus as batters bowl and 'Sandpapergate' saga rumbles on
items.summary:
England in Australia: T20 cricket the new focus as batters bowl, Adil Rashid eyes recall and 'Sandpapergate' rumbles on
England begin five-match T20 series against beleaguered Australia in Melbourne on Saturday (8.15am UK); Harry Brook's side looking to build-on ODI series win as Adil Rashid eyes re
items.text:
England in Australia: T20 cricket the new focus as batters bowl, Adil Rashid eyes recall and 'Sandpapergate' rumbles on
England begin five-match T20 series against beleaguered Australia in Melbourne on Saturday (8.15am UK); Harry Brook's side looking to build-on ODI series win as Adil Rashid eyes recall after being omitted for 50-over matches; Mitchell Marsh does not appear at pre-series press conference
Friday 20 November 2026 11:13, UK
"You could see it going horribly wrong, couldn't you? You could see things imploding."
That was Michael Atherton's take on Australia before the 'Sandpapergate' scandal spectacularly hit the headlines once again following Usman Khawaja's claims in his autobiography.
Three weeks ago, the biggest problems for the Baggy Greens were Test batting woes, including a bang-out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne, and some odd selection decisions.
They pale now, though.
- Pat Cummins under pressure after Cameron Bancroft article
- Reaction to Cameron Bancroft's incredible comments
- Listen to latest episode of Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
That "implosion" Athers predicted on the field has come off it, with David Warner and Cameron Bancroft supporting Khawaja's account that all members of the team were aware of the sandpaper scheme in 2018, and Pat Cummins strenuously denying it.
Australian cricket is at civil war and there is no obvious end in sight.
Questions abound (will Cummins survive as captain? Will Steve Smith, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood have their say? Does Cricket Australia have any choice but to launch a fresh investigation and not just an open forum?) but answers are in short supply.
England looking to pile more misery on Australia
Runs were also in short supply for Australia in the final two ODIs against England as a side helmed by Mitchell Marsh in the absence of the rested (but surely mentally tired) Cummins were twice bundled out in the low 200s chasing targets of 320-plus.
That meant Harry Brook's tourists were able to bounce back from being pummelled in Perth in the opening fixture - a result which brought back horrible memories of their Ashes thrashing at the venue a year ago - to claim a come-from-behind 2-1 series win.
They will now look to pile the misery on their beleaguered hosts with victory in a five-match T20 international series, starting in Melbourne on Saturday (first ball at 8.15am UK time).
At times in the ODIs, it felt like England were toying with an Australia team whose minds were perhaps understandably elsewhere. Jofra Archer sent out to bat at No 6 in Hobart, for example, and also Brook and Tom Banton being asked to deliver their part-time off-spin.
If Archer's elevation was a one-off - it certainly won't be seen in the T20s with the England quick rested as he prepares for the three-Test assignment in South Africa from December 17 - then the use of Brook and Banton with the ball may be a more regular occurrence, especially in 50-over cricket as Brendon McCullum's side laser in on the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
Head coach McCullum said: "These guys are talented, there is something there.
"We are looking at a World Cup in 12 months' time, and no one knows what the conditions are going to be like. You could end up on a pitch that is exploding and need some options.
"We will keep encouraging them to do that. That World Cup is potentially 13 games in three different countries, fresh pitches, there's not much data on how those pitches will play."
Marsh not expected to attend press conferences during series
Brook and Banton bowled 2.5 overs between them in the ODI series, which is 2.5 overs more than Adil Rashid. The frontline spinner had ample time to pour over the sandpaper storm after being left out for all three games, with Liam Dawson once again favoured.
Rashid will hope to be recalled for the T20s, starting at the weekend on a ground where he helped England beat Pakistan in the 2022 T20 World Cup final. The 38-year-old has played in all 19 of his side's T20Is in 2026, appearing alongside Dawson in 18 of them.
Brook, like Rashid, has fond memories of the MCG. He, too, was part of the T20 World Cup-winning squad four years ago, while he top-scored in a blink-and-you'll-miss-it, two-day Ashes Test there last winter as England claimed their only win of a sobering tour.
Brook was all smiles during his pre-series media duties in Melbourne on Friday, saying he wanted to guide his side to a 4-0 lead over Australia before he departs for the South Africa tour ahead of the series finale in Canberra on December 2.
He also spoke of his excitement that the uncapped James Coles, Henry Crocombe, Eddie Jack and Thomas Rew were able to experience being in an England squad in Australia, albeit without confirming if or when they would make their T20I debuts.
We do not know how Australia skipper Marsh is feeling, though, with the 34-year-old not expected to engage in any media activity with the written press throughout the T20 leg following Bancroft's explosive claims in that detail-filled account in the West Australian.
Marsh was part of the XI for the now infamous Cape Town Test eight years ago.
Cummins, Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc will not feature in the series at all as chat regarding what they did or did not know about the sandpaper use runs rampant.
Cummins and Hazlewood are rested, like they were for the ODIs, while Starc, who also sat out the 50-over encounters, has retired from international 20-over cricket.
Make no mistake, though. The heat is very much on them.
On the field, the heat will be on Marsh and an inexperienced bowling attack - weakened further by injuries to Mahli Beardman (quad) and Xavier Bartlett (knee) - to contain an England side that, despite missing the injured Jacob Bethell and Jos Buttler, is formidable.
Australia will also be out to avoid the top-order collapses of the final two ODIs, a goal that could be made easier by Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker joining Archer in being rested ahead of the red-ba

items.title: KCSE, KPSEA results set for January as KJSEA results target December
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Migos Ogamba has announced that the 2026 Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examination results will be released in January 2027, following the conclusion of the national examinations.
Ogamba said marking of the examination scr
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Migos Ogamba has announced that the 2026 Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examination results will be released in January 2027, following the conclusion of the national examinations.
Ogamba said marking of the examination scripts would begin promptly, with an estimated 34,170 examiners expected to handle the exercise across 41 marking centres.
The announcement comes as 1,048,355 candidates who registered for the examination in 10,693 centres countrywide bring their examination journey to a close.
Speaking on Friday, November 20, at the end of the field administration of the 2026 KCSE examinations, the CS said the exercise had been conducted over 24 days, having commenced on October 19.
He commended candidates for maintaining discipline and integrity throughout the examination period, assuring them that the Ministry would ensure credible certification of their academic performance.
“As a Ministry, we guarantee you fair and credible certification of your honest and hard work,” Ogamba said.
The examination was conducted through a multi-agency arrangement involving the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, the Teachers Service Commission and other government agencies.
Examination materials were distributed daily through 646 distribution centres to ensure their timely delivery to candidates across the country.
However, the exercise faced logistical challenges in several parts of the country, particularly areas affected by flooding and insecurity.
Ogamba cited flooding in Tana River, Kitui, Turkana, West Pokot, Wajir and Mandera as some of the challenges that threatened the smooth administration of the examinations.
Security incidents were also reported in Moyale, Isiolo, Daadab in Garissa County, as well as Kapedo and Arror in Turkana County.
The government responded by deploying helicopters and alternative means of transport to deliver examination materials to affected areas, while some candidates were temporarily relocated to safer locations to enable them to sit their papers.
The CS thanked education and security officers who worked under difficult circumstances to ensure that no candidate was denied the opportunity to complete the examinations.
KJSEA results
Meanwhile, the Ministry is prioritising the processing of the 2026 Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA), with results targeted for release before the end of December.
Ogamba said 13,484 examiners were undertaking the marking of structured questions across 24 marking centres, while machine scoring of multiple-choice questions was proceeding concurrently.
The results will facilitate the placement of learners into Grade 10 senior schools before the start of the January 2027 academic year.
The 2026 Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) outcomes are also expected in January 2027, providing feedback on learners’ performance as they transition to Grade 7.
The completion of the KCSE examinations marks the end of a critical stage in the academic calendar for more than one million candidates awaiting their final secondary school results.

The assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, triggered renewed outrage in France over police violence, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions claim is limited to isolated cases.
