Saka has been out since limping off against Bayern Munich at the end of last month, and it is understood he has yet to resume light training. Arteta revealed mor
items.text:
Mikel Arteta has said Bukayo Saka may not return before Christmas as the Arsenal forward continues his rehabilitation from a thigh injury.
Saka has been out since limping off against Bayern Munich at the end of last month, and it is understood he has yet to resume light training. Arteta revealed more tests during the international break confirmed the England forward did not need surgery and that he was expected to be out for another four weeks.
When asked whether Saka could be fit for the game against Manchester United on 20 December, Arteta was unsure. “I cannot be that specific,” he said. “In four weeks’ time a lot of things can happen. Maybe it is three and then it is five.
“At the end, there are a few elements. One is the healing of that tissue – and we cannot predict exactly when that tissue is going to be in the best condition to push it. Then there is the rehab plan that we have now, what he needs to do in the gym, what he needs to do in terms of treatment and on the field.”
Arsenal will also be without Martín Zubimendi for Saturday’s trip to Newcastle after the Spain midfielder picked up a hamstring injury against England last Sunday. Otherwise Arteta has a clean bill of health, with William Saliba poised to return after a long-term back injury, although Max Dowman remains suspended after his red card against Fleetwood.
Christos Tzolis is expected to start but Arteta revealed Arsenal’s players were now banned from selecting themselves or any teammates in the Fantasy Premier League game after the Greece forward’s team was leaked before the win over Liverpool on 1 November. Tzolis had been out injured for several weeks but picked himself for the trip to Anfield, alerting their opponents. He is believed to have played his wildcard to remove all the Arsenal players from his squad.
“We haven’t dealt with it [before] and I wanted to put new things in place,” said Arteta. “But obviously confidentiality is something critical because it’s about trust and about what you are trying to do. That should be kept as a huge secret and we’ll take measures to make sure it doesn’t happen.”

items.title: Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
items.summary:
Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for commi
items.text:
Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for committing genocide. By nine votes to six, the court found that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya crossed the gravest threshold in international law.
That matters because Myanmar’s defence was never simply that nothing terrible happened. It argued that its “clearance operations” followed attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) and were, however brutal, fundamentally counterterrorism. Genocide requires more than proof of killing, rape or village destruction; it requires specific intent to destroy a protected group.
The court found that Myanmar’s government forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, inflicted extreme violence on children and attacked people fleeing towards Bangladesh. Taking the evidence together, it concluded that the “only reasonable inference” was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
That strips away the central evasion of the past decade. The ARSA attacks were real. So was armed conflict. But rebellion is not a legal alibi for genocide. Nor can the atrocities now be dismissed as excesses by rogue soldiers. This was a judgement about what Myanmar, as a state, did to a people.
The 9-6 split will inevitably be used by Myanmar to cast doubt on the ruling. But the judgement is final and binding. And by 10 votes to five, the court went further, ordering reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, restitution of property and compensation where restitution is impossible.
For Rohingya survivors, that is extraordinary vindication. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the courtroom, called it “a great day for the Rohingya”. In Cox’s Bazar, refugees had been making an equally practical demand: They want to go home, but with rights, citizenship and dignity.
But here is the problem: You cannot eat a judgement. You cannot live inside one. You cannot rebuild a burned village with one or raise a child safely inside one.
The ICJ has no enforcement arm. Under Article 94(2) of the United Nations Charter, noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council (UNSC), where China or Russia could block action. That makes pressure outside the UNSC essential: Targeted sanctions, ASEAN diplomacy, the ICC investigation and Argentina’s universal-jurisdiction case, where arrest warrants have already been issued for 25 suspects.
Who governs the map has also changed. In 2017, Myanmar’s military dominated Rakhine. Today, the Arakan Army controls most of it, and UN investigators have documented forced recruitment, movement restrictions, arbitrary killings and other abuses against Rohingya under its rule.
Any serious return framework must therefore deal with whoever controls the ground. Bangladesh should tie cross-border trade, humanitarian access and political engagement with the Arakan Army to measurable Rohingya benchmarks: Freedom of movement, restoration of land, an end to forced recruitment, international monitoring and a pathway to citizenship. Dhaka should also press Myanmar’s authorities, ASEAN, China, India, Gulf states and Western governments to support a monitored return-and-reparations mechanism. For too long, ports, pipelines and trade corridors have been treated as “strategic” while the Rohingya remain in the humanitarian file.
Everyone wants something from Myanmar. The Rohingya should finally be part of the bill.
None of this matters if the camps fall apart before return becomes possible. About 95 percent of Rohingya refugees are moderately to highly vulnerable and rely almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. The UN’s scaled-down 2026 response plan seeks $710.5m, 26 percent less than the previous year’s appeal. In April, the World Food Programme reduced support for about two-thirds of refugees under a new tiered system; about 17 percent now receive only $7 per person per month.
Donors applauding the verdict should fund the wait as seriously as they praise the destination. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which backed The Gambia’s case, and Gulf donors have a particular responsibility. Western governments should restore cuts, while lenders and donors should support Bangladeshi host communities. Underfunded camps feed trafficking, exploitation and dangerous sea journeys towards Malaysia and Indonesia. A judgement that opens a path home is worth little if the people it was meant for cannot survive the wait.
Reparations now have legal force, not merely moral appeal. Property claims should be documented; land restored where possible; compensation paid where it cannot. Aid says: You are suffering, so we will help you survive. Reparations say: A wrong was done to you, and someone is obliged to repair it.
The verdict is enormous. The test now is simpler: Can the Rohingya go home as citizens, reclaim their land, receive compensation and raise their children somewhere other than a refugee camp?
The court has established the truth. Now justice has to bring it home.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

items.title: Was the historic Shenzhen summit a political win or humiliation for Putin?
items.summary:
Was the historic Shenzhen summit a political win or humiliation for Putin?
The world watched with bated breath Thursday as the presidents of China, Russia and the United States met for 90 minutes for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen. Each leader came to the negotiating table with their
items.text:
Was the historic Shenzhen summit a political win or humiliation for Putin?
The world watched with bated breath Thursday as the presidents of China, Russia and the United States met for 90 minutes for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen. Each leader came to the negotiating table with their own motivations. But Russia's Vladimir Putin was seen as walking away worse off than his counterparts, with some media outlets reporting the Kremlin leader was "humiliated" during the talks.
US President Donald Trump was welcomed with open arms when he visited Shenzhen, China’s “Silicon Valley”, from November 18 to 19 for a historic summit with his Chinese and Russian counterparts.
China’s President Xi Jinping went to the airport to welcome him, and he stood next to Trump in the official photo for both the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit and the opening banquet.
Read moreWhat impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?
It would have been hard for the US president to receive a more rapturous welcome.
But Trump’s Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, the third key player in this unprecedented summit, was treated almost like an afterthought.
While Xi and Trump embraced on the tarmac, Cai Qi, the Chinese Communist Party's fifth-ranking official, was assigned to welcome Putin upon arrival.
Putin kept everyone waiting
For the event's official photo, Putin was placed next to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan.
His seating arrangement for the opening banquet was equally lacking – opposite Liyuan, a former singer, and next to Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto.
Even one of Putin’s advisers, Yuri Ushakov, acknowledged that his seat placement prevented the Russian president from speaking to Trump and Xi during the meal, raising concern that these perceived snubs had ruffled Putin's feathers.
On Thursday, Putin kept Xi and Trump waiting for over an hour before joining the official opening of the historic summit that has been compared to the Yalta conference of February 1945 when the "Big Three" – Winston Churchill, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin – met to plan the postwar world.
"Putin usually likes to be late, and he has a history of this exact same kind of behaviour in diplomatic relations when things are not going his way,” said Jeff Hawn, a Russia specialist at the London School of Economics.

According to Natasha Lindstaedt, a specialist in authoritarian regimes at the University of Essex in the United Kingdom, the dynamics between this diplomatic "trio" resemble those of a mafia family gathering.
Like Don Vito Corleone in the film The Godfather – political heads of the "family" always make it crystal clear where someone stands in the hierarchy, said Lindstaedt.
"Authoritarian regimes do cooperate with each other, but they don't treat each other as equals," she said, adding that "some sort of jockeying for power takes place".
The series of diplomatic snubs directed at Putin did not go unnoticed by several Western media outlets and Russian opposition voices.
Putin "was put in his place", the Lowdown blog reported, in what the HungarianConservative referred to as "diplomatic humiliation". Russian Telegram channel Vremennoye Pravitelstvo 2.0 claimed China sought to diminish Putin through "strange diplomatic tricks".
Is Xi frustrated with Putin?
Before the summit, Putin had been referred to as Xi’s “dear friend”, but as talks began there was a stark change in attitude.
“There is a significant feeling, I think, in China that they're sick of Russia's conflict and they're unhappy with the recent ceasefire proposal on behalf of the Russians ... It shows no room for compromise. And that is irritating China because China's core objective always is increased economic growth,” Hawn explained.
By sidelining Putin in this way, Xi can ensure that he “establishes his dominance that he's the guy who Trump needs to talk to. Not Putin,” Hawn added.
Some experts said that Xi was generally frustrated with Putin, especially on the sensitive issue of North Korea.
“I think there was some irritation from the Chinese that Russia was getting so close to North Korea,” Lindstaedt said.
China wants to maintain its influence over Pyongyang’s economic and diplomatic trajectory, a role that could be threatened by Moscow and Pyongyang's military-technological cooperation.
This new rapprochement between Pyongyang and the Kremlin could provide North Korea's Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un with an alternative political ally to China.
Xi can afford to show his displeasure because “Russia needs China more than China needs Russia”, Lindstaedt said.

Stroking Trump’s ego
Other experts suggested that the pomp and circumstance laid on for Trump was more to do with stroking the US president's ego than it was about dismissing Putin.
"Trump is there for ego and for the photo opportunity. Putin is there tactically, to show that he's not isolated and to try to continue to get leverage on Ukraine ... you have his (Xi's) attempt to show that China is the responsible power now," Scott Lucas, a specialist in US affairs and international relations at the University of Dublin, said.
In this regard, “the fact this summit is taking place is a win for him (Putin)", said Richard Turcsanyi, programme director at the Central European Institute for Asian Studies (EIAS).

A drone operator who filmed Manchester United’s training session this week has apologised for what he called a “total error
items.text:
Drone operator removes Man United training footage and issues apology
The footage, filmed during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session, was uploaded online.
A drone operator who filmed Manchester United’s training session this week has apologised for what he called a “total error of judgement” and removed the footage from his YouTube channel.
The footage, filmed at United’s Carrington training ground during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session on Thursday, was uploaded online under the username “CC OVERVIEW”.
In a statement posted on his YouTube channel on Friday, the drone operator said that while the flight was legal under drone regulations, filming the session had been “unethical”.
“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time,” he said.
“I fully accept it was unethical on my part. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.”
The operator added that he had wrongly assumed only warm-up activities would be visible and that the training session would be open to various media outlets.
He also said neither Liverpool nor any other football club had been involved in his decision to film at Carrington.
“The video has been removed from my channel,” he said.
Pochettino arrived from the US men’s national team this week after United sacked Michael Carrick, and faces an immediate test with a trip to Liverpool on Sunday.
United are languishing 18th in the league table after winning just one of their 10 games. Liverpool are fourth.

items.summary:
South Korea catches 111 students with new measures against exam cheating
- Published
South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted
items.text:
South Korea catches 111 students with new measures against exam cheating
- Published
South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.
Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities said on Friday.
Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.
Prior to the Suneung, authorities announced anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.
On Friday, Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.
In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".
Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.
The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.
These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," said the candidate, 34-year-old Han Won-seok, in a video published on Sunday.
His confession, days ahead of the Suneung, prompted authorities to introduce last-minute measures to prevent cheating during the national exam.
The measures included nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea tapped on its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times that he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told news outlet Yonhap that he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
Many South Koreans see the Suneung as a culmination of years of formal education - and a turning point that determines their university placements, careers, and social statuses.

In a written interview for staff
items.text:
Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
November 20, 2026
Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."
The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.
German auto industry faces restructuring
Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.
Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.
"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."
A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."
In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.
Unions dig in amid fight for survival
Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.
Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.
Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.
"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.
China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.
Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.
Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'
A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."
PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.
These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.
"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.
With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.
Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.
"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.
Production remains resilient despite decline
Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.
Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).
IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.
In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."
Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.
Analysts call for faster reform
For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.
As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."
"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

"It is lo
items.text:
New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
New York City officials on Friday unveiled their plan to close the troubled jail complex on Rikers Island, the city's main pre-trial detention center, which has been plagued with reports of abuse and neglect for decades.
"It is long past time to close what's been a moral stain on our city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. "We cannot simply accept the old approaches to public safety just because they've always been done that way."
Rikers, which sits on a former garbage dump in the East River, has long been infamous for its dismal conditions – including crumbling infrastructure. Inmates have accused guards of excessive force, sexual assault and high rates of violence in multiple lawsuits.
Last year, a federal judge called the amount of violence at Rikers an "unconstitutional danger" for both the people held there and the staff.
Since 2022, more than 50 people have died in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. Almost all had been held at Rikers. People have been found unresponsive. They have died by suicide and been beaten to death. Federal court records say Rikers is "significantly more violent" than comparable jails.
But now, city officials say they finally have momentum to close the jail for good, and the newly released plan details how they intend to do that.
The plan — which takes on both the conditions inside the jails and the size of the population behind bars — is ambitious. It seeks to transform how the city government thinks about crime prevention and safety overall, says Insha Rahman, president of the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit.
"If New York City can do this at scale, which it will, it is encouragement for places like LA, like Chicago, like Philadelphia, like Houston to do the same," Rahman says.
A goal set by the city years ago
In 2019, the New York City Council approved a plan to close Rikers by 2027, and to build in its place four smaller jails in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx.
Rikers is on an island between Queens and the Bronx, out of sight for many New Yorkers. The borough-based jails will be closer to the courts and to public transit, making it easier for families, lawyers and service providers to visit people inside the facilities.
Since 2019, not a lot of progress has been made toward closing Rikers. City officials acknowledge they won't make the 2027 deadline. But Mamdani says the city is in a new moment.
"We're not the first administration to talk about this. We also know that the last administration had no interest in advancing this," Mamdani told NPR. "And we are also confident that we can be the first administration to deliver on it."
Earlier this year, he appointed a "Close Rikers Czar" dedicated to closing the jail and reducing the jail population. The mayor also appointed Stanley Richards as commissioner of the DOC, the first formerly incarcerated person to lead the department.
Mamdani says his administration has already taken concrete steps: The city revived plans for a housing initiative for New Yorkers released from jail with medical needs, for instance, and it opened a therapeutic housing unit at a public hospital in Manhattan.
'Human dignity at the center of incarceration'
Last year, a federal judge stripped the city of its authority over Rikers. Operations are now controlled by a remediation manager, who released his own initial plan earlier this year for bringing the jail system into legal compliance, independent of the city's plan.
Aspects of that plan took inspiration from carceral systems in Europe, a growing trend among correctional leaders across the U.S. The remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, traveled with Commissioner Richards to Germany earlier this year on a trip organized by the Vera Institute. There, they observed the country's prisons and jails, which are often regarded as an international model.
"While German correctional systems are not directly transferable to New York, they reflect a fundamentally different orientation — one that places human dignity at the center of incarceration," Deml wrote in his plan.
Last month, the Vera Institute took a second group of New Yorkers to Germany to see how jails can look when they're done right, including the Moabit jail in Berlin. Each member of that group had a part to play in reimagining New York City's criminal justice system: a prosecutor, a judge, a city councilmember, the chief who supervises officers at Rikers, among others.
At first glance, the group observed, Moabit looked like a lot of jails in the U.S., but key differences emerged on closer inspection. The jail was quiet. The cells had windows to the outside. In some of them, a door inside connected it to the adjacent cell.
"Some people are afraid of the first night here, and sometimes it really helps just to open the door to have someone to talk to," Katharina Spanaus, a staff member at Moabit, told the group.
There were also televisions in the cells to calm people down, and in the hallway, a vending machine selling cigarettes.
"I'll never forget the cigarette vending machine," says Christopher Watler, who was recently appointed chair of the New York City Board of Correction, which oversees the city's jail system.
What struck him wasn't really the cigarettes, but what the gesture communicates about treating people as human, Watler says.
It also showed him how far New York City has to go.
Just a week earlier, he sat at his first board meeting in New York, where he heard stories that evoked a different image. At the start, the board listened to anonymous phone calls from people held at Rikers.

items.text:
How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates
For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.
So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.
"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."
This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.
After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.
From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.
Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.
Trump's meme coin
Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.
Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.
In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.
A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.
Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.
For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.
Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.
A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.
"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm
But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.
Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.
The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.
Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.
The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.
Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.
Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.
"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat.
But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.
World Liberty Financial declined to comment.
Another major deal for Trump's crypto venture
Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.
Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.
The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.

items.text:
Thomas Frank: What should Crystal Palace expect from their new manager, what does he need to change - and can he keep the Eagles up?
Thomas Frank takes charge of Crystal Palace for the first time on Saturday as the Eagles face Coventry at the Coventry Building Society Arena; Frank's new side sit bottom of the Premier League table after two wins from their first 10 matches
Thursday 19 November 2026 12:21, UK
One of the Premier League's most charismatic managers is back.
On November 16, Thomas Frank signed a deal running until the summer of 2029 to take over the vacant managerial role at Crystal Palace, following the conclusion of Pierre Sage's short spell at Selhurst Park.
His return to the top flight comes nine months after he was sacked by Tottenham after a run of just seven wins in 26 Premier League games.
- Thomas Frank appointed Crystal Palace manager
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Crystal Palace news & transfers🦅
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
Before that, he had four successful Premier League seasons with Brentford, after guiding them to promotion in 2020/21.
Here, Sky Sports takes a look at what Frank needs to change, what to expect in terms of style and shape and whether he can keep Palace in the Premier League...
What situation has he walked into?
Palace won the Conference League last season, so it's easy to forget they also only finished six points above the Premier League relegation zone.
Sage was unable to build on the legacy left by Oliver Glasner, so the Eagles again find themselves in a spot of bother.
The Premier League's bottom side have lost four in succession and have the worst defensive record in the division, having conceded an average of 2.4 goals per game.
They are through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, however, and have taken five points from four Europa League league phase matches so far, which has them currently on course to qualify for the knockout rounds.
Frank highlights issues to address
Speaking in his first interview with the club, Frank identified the problems his new side need to address.
"There's no doubt - to state the obvious - we need to stabilise things. We need to work incredibly hard," he said.
"We are conceding too many goals, so we need to work on the defensive side of things, with principles, attitude. We need to work on set-pieces, which are key in both boxes. We need to work on defensive transitions, as we are conceding too many situations there.
"We need to bring energy, belief, confidence because this is a very, very good team and very good players, but they need to believe in themselves.
"We need to balance a lot of things with aiming high in Europe and two fantastic cup tournaments, but the Premier League is the most important, if we need to prioritise."
What needs to change then?
Analysis by Sky Sports News' Chris Reidy:
Frank will see areas all over the pitch he can improve for Crystal Palace, but undoubtedly his priority will be to stop them conceding as many goals and as many chances as they have so far this season.
Crystal Palace have kept one clean sheet in the Premier League this season and too often look vulnerable on transitions and weak on set-pieces.
Frank will have to review whether the personnel he has suits playing three centre-halves or if a change to four is necessary. Time and time again teams have exploited space between defenders against Crystal Palace which leads to shots or good chances created for the opposition.
Away from the defence, Frank will need to rejuvenate Adam Wharton. The midfielder has been way off his best this season, and perhaps finding the right partner for him will be key to that. Quinten Timber has shown plenty of energy and will in his early days at Palace perhaps without giving stability in the middle, and Daichi Kamada has been used higher up the pitch due to Ismaila Sarr's absence from the team.
What has gone under the radar in recent weeks because of Crystal Palace's defending, is their struggles up top. Eddie Nketiah's fortunate penalty with the last kick of the game against Liverpool spared Palace a record of four Premier League games without a goal.
Crystal Palace have spent the most time trailing in the league and have also only taken the lead in three games this season. A mentality shift is needed, because Palace have good players who aren't responding well to adversity.
What should fans expect in terms of style?
Based on his previous jobs, Frank has shown he is a pragmatic manager, not wedded to one shape or style and comfortable finding different ways to win.
His most used formation in the Premier League is a 4-3-3 (59), but he has also heavily used a 4-2-3-1 (35) or - importantly for Crystal Palace - a 3-5-2 (53).
Across his four top-flight seasons at Brentford, the Bees scored 80 set-piece goals, with only Arsenal, Liverpool and Man City scoring more across that period.
He is reportedly close to adding Bernardo Cueva - his former set-piece coach at Brentford - to his coaching staff, which suggests a similar approach is likely at Selhurst Park.
Elsewhere, while the Bees became markedly more direct after promotion from the Championship, there was still a particular focus on high quality chances, meaning fewer shots were taken from outside the box.
From 1763 shots across their first four seasons in the Premier League, Frank's Brentford created 225.0 worth of Expected Goals, which equated to a league-high 0.128 xG per shot.
So why didn't it work out at Spurs?
Analysis by Sky Sports News' Michael Bridge:
"It just didn't seem the right fit from the start. It didn't get off to the best of starts in terms of the press conference when he said: 'We will 100 per cent lose football matches.' Then he turned to the press office and said: 'Apart from Arsenal.' The problem is, when you say something at a club like Spurs, it stays.
"There were some really tough defeats for Spurs fans to look at.

items.title: Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
items.summary:
Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
The attack follows Putin’s pledge of ‘painful’ response to Ukraine’s attack on symbolic Crimean bridge.
Russia launched a barrage of air attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people, as it targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure across the country.
items.text:
Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
The attack follows Putin’s pledge of ‘painful’ response to Ukraine’s attack on symbolic Crimean bridge.
Russia launched a barrage of air attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people, as it targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure across the country.
The attacks overnight on Thursday into Friday hit vital transport bridges spanning the Dnipro River in the capital and knocked out power generation in several parts of Ukraine, officials said.
The missile and drone swarms came shortly after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin threatened retaliation for Ukraine’s targeting of a symbolic bridge linking his country with the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.
Eight people – including six in Kyiv – were killed in the overnight attacks, and 28 wounded, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said in a social media post.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ballistic missiles had damaged the Podilskyi, Darnitskyi, and Southern bridges, requiring traffic restrictions across the Dnipro.
Buildings, transport and logistics infrastructure were hit in several districts of the city, the Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement. Citywide electricity disruptions were also reported.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian sources reported that one person was killed as a strike hit a hospital in the Zaporizhia region. Nuclear power plants across the country were forced to reduce operations, causing outages in Kyiv and 10 regions, First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Friday that road and rail bridges in Kyiv used to transport weapons and military equipment to the battlefield were targeted. It added that its forces hit defence industry facilities as well as energy and transport infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.
The large-scale attack came hours after Putin pledged a “painful” response to Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch Bridge earlier this week. The attack severed the key road link across the Kerch Strait.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters on Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and United States presidents. Putin said the roadside of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and pledged to rebuild it.
Ukraine continued its efforts to target energy and military infrastructure overnight. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported that its forces had intercepted 310 Ukrainian drones.
A Ukrainian drone attack damaged an industrial facility in Russia’s western region of Smolensk, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on the Telegram messaging app, without identifying the facility.
The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said on Friday that 40 Russian oil facilities and defence industry targets have been hit over the past 50 days.
Moscow-installed officials in occupied eastern Ukraine also reported three people had been killed during an attack.
‘Unacceptable’
The overnight hostilities illustrate the lack of progress in US-led efforts to mediate a ceasefire.
US envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Russia is comfortable with Europe joining the negotiations, and also with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine that are modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
Early on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said cooperation between Ukraine, the US and Europe on negotiations is “becoming closer” and that he hoped the US would organise the first multilateral meeting involving the Europeans “as soon as possible”.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said later that a visit by three European Union representatives to Russia is “under consideration”.
However, he added that any form of Ukrainian membership of NATO is unacceptable to Moscow.
“[E]ven the notion of a formula for Ukraine’s quasi-membership of NATO, and the search for some sort of – in inverted commas – ‘creative solution’ in this area, is an option that is unacceptable to us. We discuss security guarantees first and foremost in terms of ensuring the security of our own country,” Ryabkov was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency.
“As far as Ukraine is concerned, let them recognise the irrevocable nature of our demand that this state must not join NATO. When that happens, I think the issue of security guarantees can be discussed in one way or another,” Ryabkov was quoted as adding.

COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'
- Like in previous years, the climate summit is likely to be extended until a consensus is reached
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20, 2026:
IN DEPTH — Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal
One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas.
Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.
Learn more about why fossil fuels, the main drivers of global warming, were removed from the COP31 draft declaration in this report.
COP summit poised to be extended with no deal imminent
Delegations from nearly 200 countries have been meeting in the Turkish resort city of Antalya since November 9 to negotiate ways to tackle global warming and provide financial aid to the world's poorest and most vulnerable nations to climate change.
But, as in previous years, countries remain sharply divided, and consensus has proven elusive.
Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, nations pledged to move away from fossil fuels, although no target or timeline was ever set.
Oil- and gas-producing countries have strongly resisted attempts to bring that particular issue back to the negotiating table.
Last year's COP30 summit in Brazil concluded with no mention of fossil fuels, prompting some nations to pursue the fight outside of the UN's sphere.
This year's summit is being held against the backdrop of rising living costs and the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has sent shockwaves through global energy markets and sent prices soaring.
Those challenges have taken the focus away from long-standing issues like rising global temperatures and increasingly frequent and extreme weather disasters, which have been exacerbated by this year's record-breaking El Nino.
In an initial draft deal earlier in the week, the phaseout of fossil fuels was included.
But a new draft declaration released on Thursday night by Australia, which is co-hosting the summit, omits any mention of gas, oil and coal, widely recognized as the main drivers of climate change.
The omission is a "black mark," France's Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.
Climate activists have also slammed what they call a "glaring regression."
"You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don't need to phase out fossil fuels," said Harjeet Singh, convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign.
The director of Power Shift Africa, Mohamed Adow, also condemned the slimmed-down draft text, which he said had "gone backwards."
Despite the current differences, Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, said, "We will be consulting and negotiating until it is very clear to us that we have a consensus."
IN PICTURES — Hotter seas, more plastic: High stakes for oceans
IN DEPTH — Have we missed our chance on climate?
From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?
Learn more about whether the world is acting too late to stop catastrophic climate change in this report.
Welcome to our coverage
Thank you for joining us as we bring you live updates from what is scheduled to be the final day of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey's southern Mediterranean resort city.
Like in previous years, however, it is looking increasingly likely that the negotiations will have to be extended, amid significant differences between delegates despite nearly two weeks of talks.
A new version of a joint draft declaration unveiled on Thursday night omits any mention of how to transition away from fossil fuels — the main causes of global warming.
Stay tuned as we bring you more details on those talks in this blog.

United drone update: operator issues apology
A drone operator who filmed Manchester United’s training session this week has apologised for what he called a “total error of judgment” and removed the footage from his YouTube channel.
The footage, filmed at United’s Carrington training ground during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session on Thursday, was uploaded online under the username CC Overview. In a statement posted on his YouTube channel on Friday, the drone operator said that while the flight was legal under drone regulations, filming the session had been “unethical”.
“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time,” he said. “I fully accept it was unethical on my part. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.”
The operator added that he had wrongly assumed only warm-up activities would be visible and that the training session would be open to various media outlets. He also said neither Liverpool nor any other football club had been involved in his decision to film at Carrington. “The video has been removed from my channel,” he said.
Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys… here are your 10 things to look out for in the Premier League this weekend:
Fifa news … Kozo Tashima said he hasn’t talked yet with fellow Fifa presidential race challenfer Philippe Diallo, but he’s willing to work with the Frenchman to defeat Gianni Infantino’s bid for a controversial fourth term.
Tashima and Diallo are two long-shot candidates to replace Infantino in an election set for 18 March. So there’s still plenty time to sway Fifa’s 211 member federations.
“We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he’s a great person to team up with,” Tashima said in comments translated from Japanese. “I’m not looking at Diallo as opposition. I just want to change Fifa. Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management. I do trust him. At this point I’m not think about withdrawing.”
Tashima, who repeated the words “integrity, fairness, trust and transparency” when asked why he decided to stand, is going against the endorsement of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which last month pledged support for Infantino — with Infantino on hand at the meeting in Tokyo.
“I just don’t only want to be the Fifa president, my intention was to make Fifa better,” Tashima added. “Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organisation.
“I believe the worst outcome would be for him (Infantino) to remain in office without an election,” he said. “I believe this is a test of whether Fifa truly has the capacity for self-reform. “He’s done a lot of things to make us doubt his integrity,” Tashima said, adding that income from the World Cup – or anywhere else – “is not an Infantino asset. It belongs to Fifa.”
In a three-candidate election, votes from two-thirds of the eligible members are needed to win in the first round. For the second round, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and a simple majority will win. In a two-candidate race, Infantino would need votes from 106 of the 211 member federations to win re-election.
Drone footage of Pochettino’s first training session posted on YouTube
Footage from Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United manager has appeared online after being captured by a drone operator. A 12-minute video of the session was posted on to YouTube by an account called CC OVERVIEW after being captured at United’s Carrington training ground. Pochettino and his United players can be seen in the video, with the squad having been divided into three groups.
On the post, the drone operator wrote: “For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it. The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn’t fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.
“The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the manager’s first training session, there are many media there so certainly won’t be the only footage of training released.”
Manchester United have declined to comment.
Pochettino was taking his first training session after being appointed as United’s new head coach last week, succeeding Michael Carrick who was sacked with the club in the relegation zone during this international window. Pochettino arrived in Manchester on Wednesday, having taken charge of the United States for the final time in their 2-0 win over Haiti, which finished in the early hours of Wednesday morning UK time. His first match in charge will be a visit to old rivals Liverpool on Sunday afternoon. Press Association

items.text:
Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
November 20, 2026
Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.
Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs?
This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).
The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."
"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.
At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.
How else is Lufthansa planning to save money?
The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.
Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.
The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

items.title: Guimaraes growing at Arsenal - but Arteta still wants more
items.summary:
Bruno Guimaraes: Arsenal midfielder is growing in stature but Mikel Arteta still wants more from Brazilian ahead of Newcastle return
Bruno Guimaraes is set to return to Newcastle in Arsenal colours, but even though he has worked his way into the Gunners team Mikel Arteta is still not completely happ
items.text:
Bruno Guimaraes: Arsenal midfielder is growing in stature but Mikel Arteta still wants more from Brazilian ahead of Newcastle return
Bruno Guimaraes is set to return to Newcastle in Arsenal colours, but even though he has worked his way into the Gunners team Mikel Arteta is still not completely happy; watch Newcastle vs Arsenal live on Sky Sports this Saturday from 5pm, kick-off 5.30pm
Friday 20 November 2026 09:50, UK
It's all eyes on Bruno Guimaraes this Saturday. The Newcastle hero who captained the team to cup success returns in Arsenal colours. And he returns as a growing cog in the Gunners' system.
Despite being Newcastle's key man, the Brazilian endured a slow start to life at Arsenal. An early-season injury did not help, nor did the early-season form of Myles Lewis-Skelly in the Brazilian's absence.
But now he is back in the North East as a first-choice option, having impressed in Arsenal's recent league wins over Liverpool and Hull, while also scoring crucial goals against Sunderland and Leeds.
But is Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta satisfied? Not yet.
"He's still not there," said Arteta after the 1-0 win over Hull last time out. "He's much better, he's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take the player to another level."
The comments were a surprise, given Guimaraes had just received a standing ovation from the Arsenal crowd as he was substituted following an impressive display.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Arsenal news & transfers🔴⚪
- Arsenal fixtures & scores | FREE Arsenal highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
In a largely frustrating game for the Gunners before Martin Odegaard's second-half winner, the Brazilian was at the heart of the action. He recorded more touches and passes than any other Arsenal player, while he was equally effective in the defensive side of the game.
When Arteta made attacking substitutions in search of a winner, he took Declan Rice off before Guimaraes. That is how well he was playing - but it is still not enough for the Arsenal manager.
"I told him in the dressing room - he's very good, he had a massive impact, he owned a lot of moments in the game," said Arteta. "But there is still much more to come."
Pushed on those comments this week, he said: "It's about impact, the amount of things he can do to influence the game and own the game."
To work out what Arteta is getting at, it is worth going back to the analysis the Spaniard made of his £75m signing when he first joined.
"A player which obviously has tremendous timing and intuition to win the ball back and progress play very, very fast," said Arteta back in August.
"He's a player that is very comfortable putting people through, moving between the lines, moving in behind."
Winning the ball back and playing it forward very fast are two areas where Guimaraes has excelled so far this season.
From a defensive point of view, only Chelsea's Romeo Lavia has a better ground-duel success rate this season among Premier League midfielders.
His ball-winning ability was no better seen than his roar of delight in front of the Arsenal fans in the first half of the win at Anfield, after he stopped a dangerous Liverpool attack into the penalty area.
But, as Arteta says, Guimaraes also gets the ball forward - and quickly. The numbers back that up too. He ranks very highly among Premier League midfielders for line-breaking passes.
But perhaps this is where Arteta is demanding more from the Brazilian. Rice is one of the top two or three players at line-breaking passes and Guimaraes - who plays with the England midfielder in a double pivot - has slightly lower numbers.
If Rice is the standard in Arteta's eyes, then Guimaraes has work to do to reach that level.
Another area where Guimaraes could improve is scoring goals. He netted nine Premier League goals last season and it was another key skill that Arteta identified back in August.
"He's got a smell and a really good timing to get in the box," he said. "And he has the capacity to finish the actions."
Now, Guimaraes has already shown his goalscoring prowess against Sunderland and Leeds, but they were strikes from the edge of the area. Useful, yes - but they are not classic Guimaraes goals.
Just seven of the Brazilian's Premier League goals for Newcastle came from outside the penalty area, with the remaining 24 coming from inside the penalty box. Guimaraes is yet to show the close-range threat that Arteta rates so much.
He seemingly has a lot to do to reach the levels Rice is hitting - but that is not an easy feat.
In a recent interview with GQ Magazine, Rice revealed how it can take up to a year to get used to Arteta's demands in midfield.
Rice remembered seeing Christian Norgaard - another midfielder who arrived at Arsenal with plenty of Premier League experience - struggle to keep up. "You're not going to grasp this for like six, seven months," Rice recalled about what he said to Norgaard.
Arteta recognises that too. "He's getting better at it," he said this week. "And he will get better at it when the relationships and understanding of what we do increases day by day."
"With our manager, he doesn't care who you are," Rice added. "You're getting detail. You're going into the game knowing everything."
Guimaraes is feeling that harsh side of Arteta right now. Even though he is playing and performing, there is plenty of work still to do.

The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.
Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired, external after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.
The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.
The White House has not publicly confirmed the departure or given a reason to why Cairncross left his role.

items.title: Former French prime minister Dominique de Villepin to announce presidential bid
items.summary:
Former French prime minister Dominique de Villepin to announce presidential bid
France’s former conservative prime minister Dominique de Villepin, who served as former president Jacques Chirac’s foreign minister during the country’s steadfast opposition to the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, is exp
items.text:
Former French prime minister Dominique de Villepin to announce presidential bid
France’s former conservative prime minister Dominique de Villepin, who served as former president Jacques Chirac’s foreign minister during the country’s steadfast opposition to the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, is expected to formally launch his presidential campaign Friday. But while De Villepin’s opposition to Israel’s Gaza campaign and assured analysis of international affairs has caught the eyes of younger voters, it remains to be seen if he can persuade them to cast a ballot for him.
France’s former prime minister Dominique de Villepin is expected to add his name to the already crowded list of candidates running for president in 2027, setting himself against what he describes as the country’s “extremes” as well as the competing heirs to President Emmanuel Macron’s centre-right political project.
De Villepin’s team have called a press conference for 11am at Paris’s Maison de l’Amerique Latine, founded by General Charles de Gaulle after World War II in a bid to strengthen ties between the French and Latin American republics.
The soon-to-be candidate will position himself to an alternative to “three forces relentlessly trying to cut France apart with a scalpel”, his team told AFP.
According to the former conservative prime minister, those forces are the far-right National Rally – currently leading the polls – as well as the left-wing runner-up France Unbowed and the “Macronist centre”. He accused the three groups of being responsible for France’s “decay”.
De Villepin is expected to call on voters not to resign themselves to “a death foretold” in the 2027 presidential election, instead putting himself forward as an incarnation of “renewal”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
De Villepin’s candidacy has been more than two years in the making, and the former premier has not been shy about his intention to run in recent months.
He created his own political party, “Humanist France”, published a book, built up his social media presence and travelled across the country on different speaking engagements.
Whether or not he will actually be able to stand as candidate is still uncertain. Candidates must gather at least 500 signatures from France’s mayors in order to run for office. His team maintains that De Villepin has already secured pledges from 300.
It was his failure to gather these much-needed signatures that blocked the former prime minister from running for president in 2012. Despite having stalked the halls of power since the 1980s as one of right-wing president Jacques Chirac’s chief strategists, De Villepin has never actually been elected to public office.
But De Villepin, who served as Chirac’s foreign minister during France’s steadfast opposition to US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, has built something of a following on the left as well as the right for his assured analyses of international affairs.
De Villepin’s opposition to Israel’s brutal campaign in the Gaza Strip has brought him to the attention of an electorate that would once have scorned the right-wing former prime minister – younger, and more left-leaning.
Whether or not they can actually be convinced to vote for him is another question entirely. Current polling puts De Villepin at between one to three percent.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Two people were killed in Russ
items.text:
Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack
- Published
Russia has targeted bridges in Kyiv and killed eight during one of the largest air attacks of the war so far, days after Ukraine inflicted heavy damage on the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Two people were killed in Russian strikes on a railway station in the western city of Lviv.
Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro River, vital routes which people in Kyiv rely on to move around the city, with six deaths confirmed in the capital.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The three Kyiv bridges targeted overnight - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption created by retaliatory strikes on bridges earlier this week.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary".
He added that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was also damaged and seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing the Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Ukraine's air force says almost 100 missiles were launched by Russia in its overnight attack - one of the largest attacks since the invasion began in 2022. It also involved around 400 drones.
The attack was "one of the most powerful" yet, according to Yuriy Ignat, head of communications for the Ukrainian air force.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said 28 people were injured, with an ambulance hospital in Kharkiv among the targets of an attack which hit nine regions.
Two people were killed in a hit on the Sknyliv railway station in the south-west of Lviv, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
He shared a picture of the ruined remains of what he said was the station's ticket terminal.
Ten people were injured and a rescue operation at the site is ongoing.
A Russian projectile reportedly landed inside Poland, with the armed forces searching a site 45km (28 miles) from its border with Ukraine.
Polish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued.
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
The US president dialled into the talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
