items.title: Koome reports 2.5pc drop in case backlog, says more cases cleared than filed
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — The Judiciary resolved more cases than were filed for the second consecutive financial year, reducing the overall pending caseload by 2.5 per cent, Chief Justice Martha Koome has announced.
The courts resolved 576,702 cases against 561,580 filed during the 2025/2026 financia
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — The Judiciary resolved more cases than were filed for the second consecutive financial year, reducing the overall pending caseload by 2.5 per cent, Chief Justice Martha Koome has announced.
The courts resolved 576,702 cases against 561,580 filed during the 2025/2026 financial year, achieving a Case Clearance Rate (CCR) of 103 per cent, according to the 2026 State of the Judiciary and Administration of Justice Annual Report (SOJAR).
Presenting the report on Friday, Koome attributed the improved performance to sustained efforts to enhance court efficiency, strengthen institutional systems and expand access to justice despite resource and staffing constraints.
The pending caseload fell from 595,076 cases at the beginning of the reporting period to 579,954 by June 30, 2026, while the backlog of cases pending for more than one year declined by 15.8 per cent.
However, Koome warned that 341,412 cases, representing approximately 59 per cent of the total pending caseload, had remained unresolved for more than a year, highlighting the pressure facing courts and the need to address judicial staffing shortages.
Expansion of court services
The Judiciary expanded its geographical reach during the year, establishing two new Court of Appeal stations in Kakamega and Meru, operationalising the Eldoret Court of Appeal station and opening an Embu sub-registry.
Five additional Magistrates’ Courts became operational, bringing their total to 148, while 15 new Small Claims Courts increased the national footprint to 55 stations.
Despite the expansion, 101 constituencies still lacked Magistrates’ Courts, with Koome identifying geographical access to judicial services as a continuing priority.
Alternative dispute resolution also recorded progress, with Court-Annexed Mediation reaching all 47 counties through an expanded network of 128 registries.
Of disputes valued at approximately Sh20.88 billion referred to mediation, settlements worth Sh13.05 billion were achieved without full trials.
Alternative Justice Systems were operational in 29 court stations, while 14 counties had developed county action plans to support their implementation.
Digital justice and staffing challenges
The Judiciary also reported progress in digital service delivery, with electronic filing and the Case Tracking System operational across all courts and tribunals.
A further 192,633 case files were digitised during the year, bringing the cumulative number to 749,522.
The Judiciary Contact Centre resolved 13,574 enquiries, while the pilot implementation of Mahakama AI, a legal research tool, commenced.
On staffing, the Judiciary made 1,280 appointments, including 53 Judges and 100 Resident Magistrates.
However, the institution had 8,017 employees against an approved establishment of 12,079 positions, representing a staffing level of approximately 66 per cent.
Koome said the staffing deficit continued to constrain the Judiciary’s capacity to improve case resolution timelines and expand services.
Judiciary calls for increased funding
The Judiciary’s budget increased by 19 per cent to Sh27.15 billion during the 2025/2026 financial year but remained below its operational requirements, leaving a funding gap of Sh12.95 billion.
Koome called for adequate, predictable and sustainable financing to support recruitment, infrastructure development, technological modernisation and access to justice in underserved communities.
She also highlighted the need for legislative reforms, including enactment of the Tribunals Bill and Kenya Judiciary Academy Bill, as well as reviews of the Kadhis’ Courts Act and Small Claims Court Act.
On accountability, the Chief Justice reaffirmed the Judiciary’s commitment to integrity and public trust, saying corruption, bribery, favouritism and misconduct had no place in the administration of justice.
The Office of the Judiciary Ombudsman resolved 1,111 of the 1,243 complaints received during the reporting period, representing an 89 per cent resolution rate.
Kindiki pledges government support
Deputy President Kithure Kindiki reaffirmed the government’s commitment to supporting an independent and adequately resourced Judiciary through budgetary, legislative and institutional interventions.
Kindiki said the Judiciary’s budget had increased by 19 per cent to Sh27.15 billion in the 2025/2026 financial year and would rise further to approximately Sh30.4 billion in the 2026/2027 financial year.
He cited the appointment of 53 additional Judges, enactment of the Judges’ Retirement Benefits Act, 2026, and Cabinet approval of the proposed Sh26 billion Judicial Performance Improvement Project Phase II, in partnership with the World Bank, as key interventions.
The project is intended to modernise judicial infrastructure and strengthen institutional capacity.
Kindiki also pledged government support for legislative reforms, including the Tribunals Bill and Kenya Judiciary Academy Bill, alongside a review of the Small Claims Court Act.
He said cooperation between the arms of government was necessary to ensure increased investment translated into shorter case resolution timelines, more accessible courts and greater public confidence in the administration of justice.
Lands Cabinet Secretary Alice Wahome and National Assembly Justice and Legal Affairs Committee Chairperson George Murugara, who represented Speaker Moses Wetangula, also addressed the gathering.

Manchester United: Drone operator removes footage of Mauricio Pochettino's first training session and apologises
A 12-minute video of Mauricio Pochettino's first training session at Manchester United was leaked online, showing the new head coach doing training drills ahead of Sunday's match against Liverpool, live on Sky; the apologetic drone operator says he has now taken down the footage
Friday 20 November 2026 09:25, UK
The drone operator who posted footage of Mauricio Pochettino's first training session at Manchester United on YouTube has said he has now removed the video.
The 12-minute drone footage over United's Carrington training ground showed the the Argentine overseeing various tactical drills with his new team as they prepared for their game against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.
CC Overview, who posted the footage, said on Friday morning: "I would like to speak about yesterday's incident. A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Manchester United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part. My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time.

"I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started so would have been some harmless warming up shown.
"I also wrongly assumed that the training session would have been open to various media outlets. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.
"I would also like to state that Liverpool Football Club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday. The video has been removed from my channel.
"I have spent the past four years building up my YouTube channel and were well regarded in the fields I film and would now like to get back to building up my damaged reputation and making well-received responsible videos. Thank you."
However, the video has now been shared widely across social media. The footage has been viewed over five million times on reposts from other X accounts and has since been reuploaded by several other YouTube channels, collectively attracting hundreds of thousands of views.

After the video emerged on Thursday evening, CC Overview maintained they had not broken any laws and claimed there were "many other media there".

items.title: Govt formalises Supreme Court land ownership after years without title
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Lands Cabinet Secretary Alice Wahome has handed the Judiciary title documents for the Supreme Court premises and an adjoining parking parcel, a year after Deputy President Kithure Kindiki directed the Ministry of Lands to resolve the institution’s land ownership documentatio
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Lands Cabinet Secretary Alice Wahome has handed the Judiciary title documents for the Supreme Court premises and an adjoining parking parcel, a year after Deputy President Kithure Kindiki directed the Ministry of Lands to resolve the institution’s land ownership documentation.
Wahome presented three title documents to the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) on Friday during the 2026 State of the Judiciary and Administration of Justice Report (SOJAR) presentation by Chief Justice Martha Koome, attended by Kindiki.
The handover included the title for the land occupied by the Supreme Court building in Nairobi, an adjoining parcel designated for parking and a separate property in Kapsabet.
Speaking during the presentation, Wahome disclosed that the ministry had discovered the Supreme Court did not have a title deed while processing documentation for the neighbouring parcel, which had been used as a marketplace.
“And it obviously became a security issue,” she said.
Wahome presented the original lease and certificate of lease for Nairobi Block 28/760, measuring 1.505 hectares, where the Supreme Court is situated.
The second set of documents relates to Nairobi Block 28/761, an adjoining parcel measuring 0.4759 hectares intended for parking. The land had previously been claimed by the Nairobi County Assembly.
The third title relates to a separate parcel in Kapsabet, measuring 0.7736 hectares.
“There are three titles, actually. I have one title for the Supreme Court. I have one title for the parking. And I have another title. We are working towards ensuring that the judiciary gets the title,” Wahome said.
She added that the documents had been prepared in the name of the Judicial Service Commission, departing from the previous arrangement under which titles were prepared in the name of the Cabinet Secretary for the National Treasury.
“I think the Judiciary needs to know, we prepared the titles in the name of the Judicial Service Commission instead of previous arrangement where we were preparing in the name of CS Treasury,” she said.
Wahome also said the ministry was working to secure title documentation for other Judiciary properties.
Kindiki’s earlier directive
The handover follows a directive issued by Kindiki during the 2025 State of the Judiciary presentation on November 21, when he instructed Wahome to ensure the Judiciary received its title deed before Christmas that year.
“My sister Alice, you must give the Judiciary their title deed before Christmas this year,” Kindiki said at the time.
The directive followed concerns raised by Koome over the process of securing ownership documents for Judiciary land.
Although the documents were eventually presented at the 2026 ceremony, the handover came nearly a year after the deadline set by the Deputy President.
New Supreme Court building
The acquisition of the titles is expected to support the Judiciary’s plans to expand its infrastructure, including the construction of new Supreme Court and Court of Appeal buildings.
Koome said the release of the two titles would pave the way for the planned developments, with the existing Supreme Court building earmarked for conversion into a museum.
The handover of the parking parcel is also expected to address space and security concerns around the court complex.

The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
BRUSSELS — A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.
Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.
Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.
Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be "a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security."
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be signed Friday as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people."
He said "a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe."
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.
There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain's economy.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain's independence.
"I'm afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again," Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said "it's perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?"
The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.'s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.
"Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential," Costa said ahead of the meeting. "By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond."
Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country's intentions.
Ireland's ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, "there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant." If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must "make a clear decision as to what it wants."

items.text:
Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war
Islamabad and New Delhi insist the visit is strictly multilateral, despite hopes it could open a channel for contact.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, arrived in New Delhi on Friday, becoming the first Pakistani federal minister to visit India since the neighbours fought a four-day war in May 2025.
Malik is attending the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a three-day gathering that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to inaugurate on Friday evening. Malik is expected to address the forum on Saturday.
No bilateral meeting has been announced. Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on Thursday that its participation was “reflective of its contribution as an active SCO member State to promote dialogue, cooperation and understanding in line with ‘Shanghai Spirit’”.
It is the first such visit since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari travelled to Goa in May 2023.
Both governments have framed these exchanges as routine SCO business.
With Pakistan due to host the bloc’s leaders next August, the question is how far contact confined to a multilateral forum can go — and whether this could set the stage for Modi to travel to Islamabad for the summit.
The choice of minister
Indian media, quoting diplomatic sources, reported that India’s invitation was for Pakistan’s minister for national heritage and culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi.
Neither government has confirmed this.
Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on November 6 only that it had received an invitation and would decide after consultations. Islamabad has not said why it sent Malik.
The Foreign Office said Malik would “share Pakistan’s perspective on the salience of dialogue among civilisations” and meet SCO member states on the sidelines.
Jauhar Saleem, president of the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies (IRS) and a former foreign secretary, said the choice was Pakistan’s to make.
“There is no hard and fast rule about who represents a country at such fora, and it is the prerogative of the invited state to nominate the representative it considers most appropriate,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Civilisation is not only about heritage and culture; it is about how societies relate to their land, their rivers, and one another,” Saleem added.
Khurram Dastgir Khan, a former federal minister for foreign affairs and defence and senior leader of the governing Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), said the choice was deliberate.
Sending a minister of its own choosing “lets Pakistan take part as an SCO member without being seen to buy into India’s framing or showcase,” he told Al Jazeera.
He said it also signalled Pakistan’s aim “to be seen as a constructive host for the 2027 summit; thereby nudging the door open an inch for PM Modi’s participation”.
Pakistan took over the SCO’s rotating chairmanship on September 1 and will host the leaders’ summit in Islamabad in August 2027, the month both countries mark 80 years of independence.
New Delhi’s position
New Delhi has sought to keep the visit within a narrow SCO frame.
At an October 28 briefing, foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India had invited “all SCO members” “as per established practice”, along with dialogue partners and one observer.
Asked whether New Delhi was reviewing its Pakistan policy ahead of upcoming multilateral engagements, he said: “Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place; there has been no change.”
India blames Pakistan for the April 2025 attack in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir, in which gunmen killed 26 civilians, setting the stage for the war that followed. Islamabad denies any involvement.
Sharat Sabharwal, India’s high commissioner to Pakistan from 2009 to 2013, said the invitation followed from India’s role as host.
“This is a meeting in the SCO framework, where India, as the organiser, has to invite all member countries. Therefore, at this juncture, there is no reason to look for any deeper meaning in this visit,” he told Al Jazeera.
Modi proposed the forum at last year’s SCO summit in Tianjin, China.
Irfan Nooruddin, a professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, said the initiative gave New Delhi a narrative of its own.
“If anything, it will be spun as further indication of India’s leading role in the region and its magnanimity in terms of including Pakistan in the dialogues,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rezaul Hasan Laskar, foreign affairs editor at The Hindustan Times newspaper in New Delhi, said there was little appetite at home for anything more.
“The government has maintained this is a multilateral engagement under the SCO framework, and that there will be no bilateral engagements with Pakistan till the issue of terrorism is addressed,” he told Al Jazeera. “There doesn’t appear to be widespread public backing for a fresh approach towards Pakistan.”
A history of contact
The SCO has been one of the few forums bringing the two countries together since they joined in 2017.
Bhutto-Zardari’s visit to Goa ended in public sparring. In his speech, he warned against “weaponising terrorism for diplomatic point scoring”, without naming India.
Jaishankar later described him to reporters as a “promoter, justifier and spokesperson of a terrorism industry”. The two did not hold a separate bilateral meeting.
Jaishankar’s subsequent visit to Islamabad in October 2024, for an SCO heads of government meeting, passed more quietly, with pleasantries but no talks.
In September this year, Alok Dimri, India’s SCO coordinator, spent three days in Islamabad and shook hands with Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. He described the visit to reporters as “an annual rotational ritual of the SCO”.
Dastgir said such contact had done little to change the course of relations.

items.text:
Have we missed our chance on climate?
November 20, 2026
When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.
Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.
"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.
And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.
The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.
"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."
Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.
"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.
"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.
Shoulda, woulda, coulda: Is it too late to bring temperatures under control?
The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.
The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.
A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.
"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.
Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."
He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.
Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.
"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.
But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.
The countries pushing for a fossil fuel phaseout
One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.
A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.
Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.
So far, a small but growing number of countries, including, Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.
Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."
France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.
 
Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels. 
And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.
"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

items.summary: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oc
items.text:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

items.title: Celtic look to keep Rangers at bay in title race as Frick starts Aberdeen rebuild

Scottish Premiership: Derek McInnes' Rangers on Sky, Celtic lead the way as Aberdeen begin Mario Frick era
Rangers are away to Motherwell live on Sky Sports on Saturday from 7.30pm; Celtic host St Mirren; Mario Frick's Aberdeen are at Kilmarnock; Falkirk take on St Johnstone; Dundee United are away
items.text:
Scottish Premiership: Derek McInnes' Rangers on Sky, Celtic lead the way as Aberdeen begin Mario Frick era
Rangers are away to Motherwell live on Sky Sports on Saturday from 7.30pm; Celtic host St Mirren; Mario Frick's Aberdeen are at Kilmarnock; Falkirk take on St Johnstone; Dundee United are away to Hibernian; Hearts face Dundee at Dens Park
Friday 20 November 2026 11:20, UK
The Scottish Premiership returns after the international break and with it comes the guaranteed drama.
Celtic know any slip-ups could hand Old Firm rivals Rangers the opportunity to edge closer at top of the table again.
There is a new man in charge at Aberdeen, with Mario Frick handed the challenge of turning the Dons' dismal season around.
Here, we take a look at the big talking points ahead of the weekend…
McInnes determined to avoid 'disjointed' Rangers return
Rangers head to Motherwell on Saturday evening, live on Sky Sports, aiming to carry on the momentum that has seen them win 10 games in a 12-match unbeaten run.
Derek McInnes described his team's performance following the previous international break as "disjointed" after they gave up a series of chances in a 3-1 win over Kilmarnock.
"It's something we're really mindful of, that they all go away to their different federations, they eat differently, they travel differently, they're coached differently, some are playing, some are not playing, so they get thrown out of kilter a bit," the manager said.
"So we just like to bring them together and get that focus again on what we're doing here at the club and the importance of knuckling down, being focused to win this game."
Their opponents are unbeaten in their last three after a run of seven defeats, with boss Alfred Johansson confident his squad is finally getting to the position he wanted before the season started.
Paul McGinn, Callum Hendry and Oscar Priestman have returned from injury off the bench in recent weeks and Alex Lowry could make a comeback against his former club.
Will Celtic continue to build momentum?
After taking the last international break to consider his future after three consecutive defeats in all competitions, Martin O'Neill returns from this one with a more positive outlook.
They are four points clear of Rangers, albeit having played a game more, ahead of welcoming St Mirren to Parkhead.
O'Neill has already said there are "things that we can definitely do much, much better," but against a team who have won just one of their last six league games, he will be feeling positive.
Kasper Hogh is one player who could "do better" as he struggles to live up to his record transfer fee.
The striker has played 18 games since joining Celtic for £11m and scored in just one - a hat-trick against Kilmarnock back in August.
A new beginning at Aberdeen
New manager Frick is intent on making Aberdeen a more prolific team as he bids to enjoy the type of longevity at Pittodrie that he had at previous club Luzern.
The 52-year-old former Vaduz boss has been appointed as Stephen Robinson's successor and will take charge of his new team for the first time in Saturday's bottom-of-the-table showdown at Kilmarnock.
The 11th-placed Dons are the joint-lowest scorers in the Scottish Premiership, with just 12 goals from 12 league games.
"I'm known for high-scoring clubs," Frick said as he faced the media for the first time since his appointment. "Two times with Vaduz we had a high-scoring goal record.
"Aberdeen is lacking to score, and so I'm here to change that.
"We need time, but we don't have it, so more important now is to show the basics. Body language, willingness to work, aggression, intensity - that's what I and the supporters want to see in Kilmarnock."
While the new boss is targeting the top-six, defeat at Rugby Park would see them end the weekend bottom of the table.
Killie have their own issues - they have managed just one home win in the Premiership so far this campaign. If Frick makes a winning start, they will be cast five points adrift.
Will Falkirk pick up where they left off?
Falkirk are on a five-game winning run during which they have beaten champions Celtic and ended Hearts' incredible 19-month unbeaten run at Tynecastle Park.
The Bairns return to action against St Johnstone sitting third in the Scottish Premiership - at the last international break, they were down in 11th after winning just one of their first six games of the season.
Their last win before the break came at a cost though, with captain Brad Spencer ruled out until the end of January after having surgery on a knee injury suffered against Hearts.

items.summary:
KISUMU, Kenya, Nov 20 — Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo has urged young people in the Nyanza region to acquire national identity cards and take advantage of government empowerment programmes to improve their livelihoods.
Omollo said identification documents were essential for accessing g
items.text:
KISUMU, Kenya, Nov 20 — Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo has urged young people in the Nyanza region to acquire national identity cards and take advantage of government empowerment programmes to improve their livelihoods.
Omollo said identification documents were essential for accessing government services and economic opportunities, beyond their use in voter registration.
Speaking during a meeting with youth representatives from Siaya, Kisumu, Migori and Homa Bay counties under the Kenya Youth Transition Initiative (KYTI) in Nyakach, Kisumu County, the PS said identity cards enabled young people to access education, healthcare, financial services and business opportunities.
“An identity document is not just for the sake of it. It gives our people dignity, it gives them identity. But more than that, it allows them to actively participate and take charge of their own lives,” said Omollo.
Accompanied by Kisumu County Commissioner Ronald Mwiwawi, he challenged KYTI coordinators to work with officers from the National Registration Bureau and National Government Administration to help young people without identity cards obtain the documents.
He also urged those who already had identity cards to register as voters through the ongoing continuous voter registration exercise and participate in the planned mass voter registration exercise next year.
Omollo said KYTI had mobilised more than 8,000 young people across the four counties, providing a platform to connect them with government services and development opportunities.
He cited the National Youth Opportunities Towards Advancement (NYOTA) programme as one of the initiatives targeting young people through business support, skills training and economic empowerment.
According to the PS, more than 133,000 young people across the country had benefited from business support under NYOTA, while the expanded NYOTA Access to Government Procurement Opportunities (AGPO) programme had attracted more than 300,000 registrations against a target of 600,000.
“Through the NYOTA AGPO programme, over 300,000 have already registered. The target is 600,000 young Kenyans who will be taken to training, supported to open their companies, supported to get business with government and funded to deliver on those business opportunities,” he said.
He encouraged KYTI members interested in entrepreneurship to pursue the opportunities, acquire relevant skills and take an active role in building sustainable businesses.
The PS also urged young people to pursue further education and professional development, challenging them to advance beyond their current academic qualifications.
“If you have a high school certificate, you need to get a diploma. If you have a diploma, you need to get a degree. If you have a first degree, you need to get your master’s,” he said.
Omollo further cautioned young people against drug and alcohol abuse and involvement in criminal activities, saying such behaviour could undermine their ambitions.
He challenged KYTI members to become role models in their communities by mentoring younger people, supporting those facing difficulties and working with local administrators to address challenges affecting the youth.
“As KYTI, you must lead the way by being the good role model of who a young person in Nyanza region needs to be,” he said.
He particularly urged the youth to support school-going children during the holiday period and help prevent teenage pregnancies, drug abuse and other challenges that could disrupt their return to school in January.
Omollo also encouraged young people to engage government leaders and administrators for mentorship and guidance, while emphasising the importance of civic education in helping them understand government structures, their responsibilities as citizens and available development programmes.
The meeting brought together KYTI county, constituency, ward and polling station coordinators as part of efforts to strengthen youth participation, access to government services and inclusion in national development.

items.text:
Iraqi security forces deploy in Hezbollah stronghold under compromise deal
Iraqi security forces deployed in the Kataib Hezbollah stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, state media said on Friday, under a compromise deal brokered by Shi'ite politicians. Iraq's prime minister ordered a security intervention earlier this week after accusing the Iran-backed militia of smuggling state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Iraqi security forces have deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, on Friday, state media said, under a compromise deal designed to ease tensions with Iran's most powerful Shi'ite militia ally in the country.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi earlier this week ordered security forces to prepare to move against Kataib Hezbollah, which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Under the deal, brokered by Shi'ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq, a major oil producer and ally of both the United States and Iran.
Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United States, has rejected the smuggling accusations. So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, a Kataib stronghold about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad.
Any direct confrontation with Iran's heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky.
After one of Zaidi's predecessors ordered a similar crackdown on militias five years ago, the prime minister's Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt.
US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran at the end of February. Kataib Hezbollah and other militias have refused to hand over their weapons to the state.
Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib Hezbollah, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters.
It forms several battalions in Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and subsequently recognised as an official security force.
Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF.
While it is technically under the command of Iraq's prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command and has defied and challenged government statements calling for an end to attacks on US forces.
Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though the group denies this and says it is dedicated to security.
In August, Iraqi special forces reporting directly to the prime minister arrested the intelligence chief of the Iran-aligned faction Harakat al-Nujaba on accusations of involvement in drone attacks against US interests.
The detention, which lasted 48 hours, triggered threats of retaliation from the group and prompted intervention by senior Shi'ite politicians who helped defuse tensions. A week later, Iraqi special forces arrested four militia members over allegations they facilitated attacks on US interests.
(FRANCE 24 wirh Reuters)

items.title: Gates Foundation Africa chief Dr. Basinga urges Africa to prioritise practical AI solutions
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Africa must prioritise investment in basic services and develop evidence-based artificial intelligence solutions that address local needs, rather than deploy technology for its own sake, Gates Foundation Africa Director Dr. Paulin Basinga has said.
Basinga cautioned against
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Africa must prioritise investment in basic services and develop evidence-based artificial intelligence solutions that address local needs, rather than deploy technology for its own sake, Gates Foundation Africa Director Dr. Paulin Basinga has said.
Basinga cautioned against overreliance on artificial intelligence, saying technology should support people in addressing challenges rather than become an automatic response to every problem.
“It is not every time you need to deploy AI. Sometimes you can actually solve the problem yourself. AI is there to assist you,” he said.
He was speaking during discussions on the future of agentic artificial intelligence in Africa at a Nairobi meeting that brought together innovators, policymakers and other stakeholders to explore the continent’s role in shaping emerging AI technologies and standards.
Basinga said AI could help African countries improve efficiency across sectors, particularly healthcare, where it could support overstretched health workers, reduce medical errors and improve the distribution of medicines.
However, he warned that technology could not substitute investment in basic services, emphasising the need for countries to build the data, skills and evidence required to develop and deploy AI solutions effectively.
His remarks came as African innovators showcased applications of agentic AI capable of addressing challenges across sectors, including education.
Kenyan education technology startup Dira won the Education track at the African Agentic AI Design Challenge, taking home US$10,000 for its AI-driven solution designed to help teachers identify learners who need additional attention and provide tailored support.
Founded by Irene Mukii, Jacinta Wanjiru and Michelle Gati, Dira was among the winners announced at the “Agentic AI for the Global South”, a closed-door side event held on the margins of the MCP Dev Summit in Nairobi.
The startup developed an AI assistant integrated into teachers’ daily workflows, helping them identify learners who may need support and convert quick spoken observations into structured “Evidence Cards”.
The system searches educational research to suggest interventions tailored to individual learners’ needs, learning styles or potential disabilities, while allowing teachers to retain control by approving or rejecting updates.
Marga AI emerged as the first runner-up, winning US$8,000, while TALO was the second runner-up developed by university students aged 21 and 22, was the second runner-up, receiving US$6,000. All three teams also received computing credits.
The challenge showcased more than 60 AI agents developed by innovators, highlighting the growing application of agentic AI to problems facing the continent.
The workshop, held on November 18 at the Hyatt Hotel in Nairobi, focused on how Africa can help shape the rules governing agentic AI instead of being left to adapt to standards developed elsewhere.
Participants argued that early engagement by policymakers could help prevent fragmented regulations across countries while strengthening collaboration between governments and innovators.
The discussions examined what it takes to develop, deploy and govern AI while ensuring solutions respond to local needs.
The Gates Foundation is placing greater emphasis on ensuring AI benefits communities historically underserved by technological advances.
The foundation has committed at least US$1 billion over the next two years to expand access to AI and AI-enabled solutions. Of the funding, 40 per cent is directed to healthcare, another 40 per cent to education, 10 per cent to agriculture and 10 per cent to digital foundations.
Basinga’s remarks underscored the need for African countries to balance technological ambition with investment in foundational services, while ensuring they have the skills, data and capacity to shape AI solutions for their own development priorities.

items.title: Erasmus running risk of breaching World Rugby ban with watchalong
items.summary:
Rassie Erasmus: Sky Sports understands South Africa head coach running the risk of breaching suspension with watchalong
Sky Sports understands Rassie Erasmus would be running risk of breaching six-Test World Rugby suspension with planned watchalong of Saturday's Ireland vs South Africa Nations Champ
items.text:
Rassie Erasmus: Sky Sports understands South Africa head coach running the risk of breaching suspension with watchalong
Sky Sports understands Rassie Erasmus would be running risk of breaching six-Test World Rugby suspension with planned watchalong of Saturday's Ireland vs South Africa Nations Championship Test; part of Erasmus' ban covers "direct or indirect contact with team management on matchdays"
Friday 20 November 2026 08:41, UK
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus would risk breaching the terms of his six-Test ban if he holds his planned online watchalong of Saturday's Nations Championship clash with Ireland, Sky Sports understands.
Erasmus is serving a six-match suspension handed down by World Rugby following extraordinary claims, saying "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby after his side's defeat to France in Paris last week.
The 54-year-old was suspended for "public criticism of match officials, undermining the integrity of individuals or the sport, and fuelling online abuse", but has since taken to X to confirm he will watch Saturday's Test from his Dublin hotel room and has organised a free watchalong for anyone to sign up and view him react to the Test match as it is unfolding.
Erasmus' ban covers the following:
"The suspension applies with immediate effect, applies to international matches, and includes any matchday involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays; entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure, technical area, approaching and/or communicating with match officials on matchday; engaging in any 'feedback' process with match officials; and engaging in media duties during the suspension."
- England's All Blacks acid test, Erasmus circus, Boks to storm Dublin?
- Sheehan starts at No 8 for Ireland vs Springboks as Prendergast plays
- Banned Springboks coach Erasmus invites fans to watch-along of Ireland game
- Springboks boss Erasmus given six-game ban for 'match-fixing' claims
Regarding the "direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays" element of his suspension, Sky Sports sought guidance on the potential for one of South Africa's coaching staff or management set-up signing up and listening to and watching the reactions and comments of their suspended head coach during Saturday's contest - something which could have a bearing on prospective replacements and tactics in the Test.
While this specific scenario is not covered by the guidelines, Sky Sports understands Erasmus' plan could be considered a breach by rugby's governing body.
It is also understood there would be a delay to any broadcast feed Erasmus will be using.
South Africa Rugby released a statement requesting a full misconduct hearing in an immediate response to the sanction, but it is understood formal confirmation of an intention to appeal is yet to be received at World Rugby.
Erasmus has now been suspended three times in five years for these sorts of incidents.
During the 2021 British and Irish Lions series in South Africa, after the Springboks lost the first Test, Erasmus broadcasted an hour-long critique of Australian referee Nic Berry, and was eventually handed a two-month ban from all rugby activity and 10-month matchday ban.
In 2022 he received a two-Test ban after sarcastic social media posts following back-to-back South Africa defeats to Ireland and France. A video critical of referee Wayne Barnes led to the official revealing he and his family had received death threats.
On Wednesday, SA Rugby released a statement "condemning the online abuse of officials" following confirmation of Erasmus' ban.

items.summary:
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term after constitution change
Critics accuse populist president of engineering a de facto one-party state in El Salvador.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched a re-election campaign that critics say illustrates his bid to make El Salvador a o
items.text:
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term after constitution change
Critics accuse populist president of engineering a de facto one-party state in El Salvador.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched a re-election campaign that critics say illustrates his bid to make El Salvador a one-party state.
Supporters gathered outside the Supreme Electoral Tribunal on Friday as Bukele arrived to register his candidacy for the February elections.
The populist is widely expected to win the race thanks to the huge political support earned by his crackdown on El Salvador’s violent cartels.
However, the launch of the campaign comes after his party Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in the country’s congress to remove term limits on the presidency and extend the length of terms from five to six years.
Critics accuse the president of consolidating power by removing checks and balances. The Bertelsmann Transformation Index and others accuse Bukele of creating a de facto one-party state.
The 45-year-old has made uprooting El Salvador’s cartels a core part of his presidency and political persona.
“In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy,” Bukele told the crowd on Friday. “We’re sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past.”
He has now begun exporting the model. Last month, he sent about 2,500 soldiers to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a United Nations-backed force went missing. The deployment has been welcomed by gang-wracked Port-au-Prince.
However, many analysts question Bukele’s motives, accusing him of exploiting the crisis on the island nation to enhance his reputation.
“Bukele is running for a third consecutive term after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticise him,” Juan Pappier of Human Rights Watch said, according to The Associated Press news agency.
“The absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration.”
Last year, Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in Congress to abolish second-round votes and bring forward national elections by two years, to February 2027.

items.text:
India: Pakistani minister visits Delhi for SCO forum amid frozen ties
November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Pakistani minister is in Delhi for SCO forum, the first ministerial visit since 2023, even as the opposition questions PM Modi's government
- US religious freedom panel has accused India of targeting Muslims in voter roll revision, urging a 'country of particular concern' label
- Cyclone Akvan has made landfall along India's eastern coast,
Here is a roundup of headlines from India from Friday, November 20:
Pakistani minister in Delhi for SCO forum, first ministerial visit since 2023
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) cultural forum.
It is the first visit to India by a Pakistani federal minister since Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023, and the first since last year's conflict between the two countries.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to inaugurate the Civilizational Dialogue Forum, which runs from November 20 to 22. India invited Pakistan's culture minister in October, but Islamabad sent Malik instead.
Pakistan's Foreign Office said he would present the country's views on dialogue among civilizations and meet other SCO members on the sidelines, local media reported.
Malik said the visit is not a bilateral negotiation, according to NDTV. No breakthrough in frigid relations is expected.
The visit comes after the four-day India-Pakistan conflict of 2025, set off by the Pahalgam attack, which killed at least 70 people on both sides, AFP stated. It also comes two days after Indian forces killed Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat.
Opposition leaders criticized the government's move to host Malik.
"BJP always says that talks and terrorism cannot happen at the same time. But now, a Pakistani minister is visiting India for the SCO meeting," said Samajwadi Party leader Fakhrul Hasan Chand, NDTV reported.
Congress Member of Parliament Pramod Tiwari also recalled Malik's earlier remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty, calling his language that of a "terrorist," according to NDTV.
Earlier this year, Malik, referring to the Indus Waters Treaty suspension after last year's Pahalgam terror attack, had warned against "water aggression," pressing India to respect the 1960 treaty.
"Whoever touches our water, their hands would be cut off," he said at the time.
US religious freedom panel says India targeted Muslims in voter roll revision
The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) said Thursday that India has escalated its targeting of religious minorities during a voter list revision that struck off tens of millions of names, Reuters reported.
At 130 million names removed, it is the largest deletion in India's history, local media reported.
"The Indian government is targeting Muslim citizens by removing them from voter rolls, calling them 'foreigners,' and now illegally deporting them," USCIRF chair Asif Mahmood said in a statement.
The revision has become entangled with a separate drive to identify and expel suspected illegal immigrants, even though removal from the rolls does not itself establish that someone is a foreigner.
USCIRF commissioner Gene Mills urged the State Department to designate India a "country of particular concern."
The panel is a bipartisan US government body whose recommendations are not binding, and Washington has not acted on its recent ones on India.
India's Election Commission is overseeing a nationwide re-verification of the electoral rolls requiring voters to prove their eligibility to remain on them, removing duplicate, deceased, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters.
But critics say the ECI has gone far beyond that remit.
The Indian Express reported that more than 130 million names were removed from electoral rolls across the country. Before this, India had some 970 million eligible voters.
For scale, Germany has about 60 million eligible voters in total.
India's Foreign Ministry has cast USCIRF as biased, and New Delhi has called such criticism interference in its internal affairs.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to our Friday coverage!
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again, bringing you the latest news out of India.
As Prime Minister Narendra Modi prepares to kick off the First Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue Forum in the national capital on Friday, the arrival of an unlikely guest is raising questions.
A US government religious freedom panel says India's voter list revision, which removed an estimated 130 million names, targeted Muslims, while the Election Commission has said it removed duplicate, deceased and ineligible voters.
Meanwhile, Cyclone Akvan has made landfall along India's eastern coast, the third cyclone to hit the region within a month.
For this and more, follow our live blog.

items.title: Gilgil MP Martha Wangari defects to DCP amid high-profile exits from UDA
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Gilgil Member of Parliament Martha Wangari has defected from President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA) party to former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), adding to a growing list of lawmakers abandoning the ruling outf
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Gilgil Member of Parliament Martha Wangari has defected from President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA) party to former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), adding to a growing list of lawmakers abandoning the ruling outfit.
Wangari, who also serves as a member of the Speaker’s Panel, switched allegiance to DCP on Friday after being received by Gachagua at his Wamunyoro residence.
Announcing the defection, Gachagua said the lawmaker had received instructions from her constituents to join DCP and use the party as her political vehicle in the 2027 General Election.
“Hon. Martha has received express instructions from the people of Gilgil to join the party of the moment, DCP, and use it to vie for her seat in 2027,” Gachagua said.
The former Deputy President urged Wangari to prepare for the party’s nominations scheduled for March next year, signalling that DCP intends to begin its candidate selection process ahead of the next election.
He described her arrival as a boost to the party’s growing membership and reiterated that DCP remained open to politicians seeking an alternative political platform.
Wangari’s defection comes days after Gachagua received three other sitting MPs who abandoned UDA for DCP: Gatundu South MP Gabriel Kagombe, Laikipia West MP Wachira Karani and Nyeri Woman Representative Rahab Mukami.
The three lawmakers were received at Wamunyoro on November 17, with Gachagua describing the political developments as a defining moment for Mt Kenya politics.
“All politics is local. A defining moment for Mlima politics,” he said at the time.
He also declared that DCP was open to politicians joining the party without conditions.
“I welcome all leaders who wish to join our party and come back home unconditionally,” he said.
Gachagua announced that the party’s recruitment window would remain open until December 31, 2026, giving politicians time to leave their existing parties ahead of the 2027 elections.
He further claimed that DCP had grown from 19 members to 25 following the latest political movements and expressed confidence that it would attract more elected leaders.
“The DCP team has grown from 19 members to 25. I have no doubt that we will have 60 MPs by next year,” he said.
Wangari’s entry adds to DCP’s efforts to establish itself as an alternative political vehicle in the Mt Kenya region, which was a key support base for President Ruto in the 2022 General Election.
Other prominent politicians who have joined the party include Murang’a Governor Irungu Kang’ata, Nakuru Senator Tabitha Karanja and Nyandarua Governor Kiarie Badilisha.
Gachagua has been seeking to consolidate his political influence in the region following his fallout with Ruto and subsequent impeachment as Deputy President in October 2024.
The former Deputy President has increasingly positioned DCP as a rallying point for leaders seeking to challenge UDA’s influence in the region ahead of the 2027 polls.

items.title: Khawaja branded 'biggest traitor ever' in Sandpapergate fallout
items.summary:
Australia's Sandpapergate: Usman Khawaja called 'traitor' by former South Africa bowler for ball-tampering claims
Ex-South Africa bowler Fanie de Villiers says Usman Khawaja "broke every single code of conduct" with allegations in autobiography; Khawaja's claims since backed up by David Warner, Chad
items.text:
Australia's Sandpapergate: Usman Khawaja called 'traitor' by former South Africa bowler for ball-tampering claims
Ex-South Africa bowler Fanie de Villiers says Usman Khawaja "broke every single code of conduct" with allegations in autobiography; Khawaja's claims since backed up by David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft; Dr Simon Longstaff feels Pat Cummins' denial of knowledge is "sincere"
Friday 20 November 2026 08:42, UK
Former South Africa bowler Fanie de Villiers has branded Usman Khawaja "the biggest traitor he's ever seen" after the ex-Australia batter's allegations about the Sandpapergate affair.
Khawaja said in his autobiography that every member of the Australia team was aware of the plot to manipulate the ball with sandpaper on the 2018 South Africa tour, a claim backed up by David Warner, Chadd Sayers and, most explosively, Cameron Bancroft.
Bancroft - who, along with Warner and then-captain Steve Smith, served a ban following the rumbling of the ball-tampering plot - wrote in a 4,000-word-plus article in the West Australian newspaper that Pat Cummins' vehement denials made him break his silence.
- Pat Cummins under pressure after Cameron Bancroft article
- Cameron Bancroft article blows Sandpapergate open
- Reaction to Cameron Bancroft's incredible comments
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
Current Australia Test skipper Cummins stated in a 68-minute press conference last week that Khawaja's claims were "utter nonsense", which Bancroft said left him feeling "angry, betrayed and alone".
De Villiers, who played 18 Tests and 83 ODIs for South Africa between 1992 and 1998 told Perth's 91.3 SportFM, that Khawaja had "broken every single code of conduct".
The 62-year-old said: "I want to go on the record and say I think Khawaja is probably the biggest traitor that I've ever seen ... over my last 40, 50 years of watching the game.
"He's sold out his fellow players. This is not about right or wrong. The wrong has already been handled. It's already been part of Australian cricket, and it's sad that it happened.
"But this guy has brought everything to the fore again.
"He's brought Australian cricket in disrepute all over again, breaking down of friendships, the code of conduct that one has within the team, he's done everything wrong one can think of."
'I believe Cummins was sincere in press conference'
Dr Simon Longstaff, part of the cultural review into Australian cricket that Cricket Australia sanctioned after Sandpapergate, says he did not think Cummins was lying in his fiery press conference but also believes Bancroft's account of the saga.
"I think both (Cummins and Bancroft) have been sincere in what they're saying," Longstaff told Australian broadcaster Nine.
"It's possible, that as a very young, inexperienced bowler at the time, (Cummins) was having conversations about the ball without understanding the conditions under which it was being altered. That has got to be allowed still as a possibility.
"I've been around long enough and have investigated various problems of this kind, where people have sworn black and blue that they were telling the truth, and you eventually find out that they both were being sincere.
"It's possible to utter what is objectively false but not do so with any kind of inclination to lie, so I think it's something still in the middle of that that needs to be explored.
"What is clear now is that the whispers that I was hearing at the time line up pretty much with what Bancroft has said, including the timing for the first use of sandpaper.
"What's distressing is that when people were given the opportunity to tell the truth, including by me, they chose not to do so. And that's a stain that carries across to the team to this day."
Former England captain Michael Atherton said on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast that he does not expect Cummins to resign from his role as Test skipper.
Atherton said of the 33-year-old: "He's obviously got a lot of credit in the bank in terms of performance as captain, having transformed the culture and kept Australia at the top of the tree, if you like.
"So I don't think there's an immediate threat there."

items.title: What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season
items.summary:
The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged.
Across th
items.text:
The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged.
Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing.
There have inevitably been outliers. Tottenham have tumbled by at least 10 places after matchweek 10 in the past two seasons and Newcastle (in 2021-22), Crystal Palace and Everton (both 2017-18) have risen from the relegation zone at this point to the safety of mid-table by May.
But even moving one position across the remainder of the season can make an enormous difference to a team on the fringe of the Champions League qualification spots, or to those that sit 17th or 18th after 10 games. Not since 2006-07 have the bottom three clubs with 28 matches to go all been relegated.
This fact feels especially relevant this season given two of the three teams in the drop zone have changed their manager since the previous round of matches. Sunderland have stood by Régis Le Bris but he is the favourite to be the next Premier League manager to leave their post. If we can reasonably assume at least one of the clubs currently 18th to 20th will be in the top flight in 2027-28, which is best placed to survive?
It is going to be very tough for Crystal Palace. Opta’s underlying data model implies they are where they deserve to be in the table, whereas Manchester United and Sunderland should be much higher. The largest improvement Palace’s new manager, Thomas Frank, engineered between weeks 10 and 38 at Brentford was two places, which will not cut it this season. Palace have to take inspiration from the 2024-25 season, in which they also had seven points after 10 games yet rose to finish 12th.
Mauricio Pochettino’s Chelsea were 11th going into their 11th game in 2023-24 before ending sixth. As they were also 11th in early April, they made a much shorter dash to the finish line, though. Pochettino’s teams usually improve as campaigns wear on, with Tottenham rising three places after week 10 in each of his first three seasons with the club. A similar lift in his new role would not make this season a rousing success for United but it would stave off the unthinkable idea of relegation.
For someone to escape, someone else must take their place. Ignoring the possibility that the answer to “who?” may be Manchester City, the team in 17th are inevitably the ones most at risk. Of the 13 sides in the past decade who were outside the drop zone after 10 games but went down, six were fourth-bottom going into matchweek 11.
Given that the points gap between first and 20th (20) was last lower at this stage in 2015-16, those figures may be more pertinent than position this season. Leeds in 2022-23 and Bournemouth three years earlier had 13 points after 10 games but were relegated, as did Blackpool in 2010-11 and Middlesbrough two seasons before them.
Only nine clubs are now above that bar, with Aston Villa, Newcastle and Tottenham among those who are not. The table is unlikely to change too much before the end of the campaign but there is a distinct chance that a secure-looking side will perish.

items.title: How West Ham striker's testicular cancer tragedy is educating next generation
items.summary:
How the story of Dylan Tombides is helping educate FIFA U17 World Cup players about testicular cancer
Mother and brother of former West Ham and Australia youth team striker Dylan Tombides have partnered with FIFA to raise awareness of testicular cancer; Visit dt38.org to find out more about DT38 Fou
items.text:
How the story of Dylan Tombides is helping educate FIFA U17 World Cup players about testicular cancer
Mother and brother of former West Ham and Australia youth team striker Dylan Tombides have partnered with FIFA to raise awareness of testicular cancer; Visit dt38.org to find out more about DT38 Foundation, Dylan's story and advice and guidance about testicular cancer.
Thursday 19 November 2026 22:10, UK
Fifteen years on from West Ham striker Dylan Tombides discovering he had testicular cancer at the U17 World Cup, his mother and brother are back at the tournament delivering inspiring, emotional talks to the current generation of players to raise awareness in his honour.
Tombides passed away in April 2014 aged just 20, following a battle with the cancer he was diagnosed with while on international duty with Australia's youth team in Mexico in 2011.
A random drugs test revealed what had originally been misdiagnosed by his GP as a cyst was far more serious. Three years of "really intense chemotherapy" followed, says his mother Tracy.
The DT38 Foundation was set up in his name and, in partnership with FIFA Medical, Tracy and Dylan's brother Taylor are part of the initiative at this year's tournament in Doha to explain to players why regular self-examination matters and how to carry it out.
"Getting the call from FIFA was a massive opportunity and an amazing thing for us and for the charity," says Taylor. "Obviously, it's where Dylan last kind of played healthy before his diagnosis. So to come back to where it all started for us as a family is a grateful honour."
During two weeks of talks to 48 teams, Tracy and Taylor have presented to 1,200 players.
With testicular cancer the most common cancer in males aged 15 to 44 - but highly treatable and in most cases curable when detected early - the importance of the sessions could be life changing.
"It's the number one cause of fatality of cancer in this particular age group," explains Dr Andy Massey, FIFA's Chief Medical Officer, who helped form the partnership and has overseen the provision of free scans to players during the tournament.
"This is one of the biggest things I think I've ever done in my sports medicine career because it has such a reach."
Tracy and Taylor's accounts of Dylan's stories have had a powerful impact on their audiences.
"One of the young players stood in front of me and said, 'I'm so sorry for your loss. I'm sorry your son isn't coming home to you. We are so grateful that you are telling us all about it'," says Tracy, recounting a talk with the Jamaican team. A similarly emotional conversation with the French squad ended in hugs instead of handshakes.
The DT38 Foundation have a campaign called Check One Two, encouraging men to check themselves on the first day of every month. Dylan's nickname 'Didge' also provides an acronym and hashtag for the foundation: Delay Is Deadly, Get Educated.
"Early detection is the difference between dealing with cancer treatment that has a 96 per cent cure rate or the figures drop away very, very quickly if you have to go to round two or round three of chemotherapy," says Tracy, who also encourages men with concerns to "insist on an ultrasound" test.
Tracy and Taylor treasure "messages that we've got from people who say, 'I thought of Dylan's story when I found a lump and I knew not to delay. I had testicular cancer and now I'm cancer-free and Dylan saved my life'."
"That tells us that what we're doing is life-changing for that family, that person," says Tracy.
Taylor believes they can have an impact through generations, too. "The effect is lasting. If we can teach these kids now, we know the next generation, they'll teach their kids and they'll teach their kids and it'll be continuous," he says.
"We're not just affecting one life, we're affecting a whole generation of lives, which is the biggest part of it. Without FIFA, we couldn't touch as many people as we have."
Visit dt38.org to find out more about the DT38 Foundation, Dylan's story and advice and guidance about testicular cancer.
