items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Detectives have arrested four suspects in connection with a brutal machete attack on Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya’s communications officer and blogger Amos Masika Boaz, popularly known as Hammer Hammer, whose vehicle was torched during a night-time ambush at his hom
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Detectives have arrested four suspects in connection with a brutal machete attack on Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya’s communications officer and blogger Amos Masika Boaz, popularly known as Hammer Hammer, whose vehicle was torched during a night-time ambush at his home.
The four were arrested in Kiminini Town following a coordinated manhunt by detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) Operations Support Unit and officers drawn from Trans Nzoia East, Trans Nzoia West and Kiminini.
The attack occurred on the night of November 16, 2026, at Orombe Farm in Trans Nzoia East Sub-County, shortly after Masika arrived at his compound.
According to the DCI, two masked assailants armed with machetes confronted the blogger, dragged him out of his silver Honda, registration number KDD 938D, before dousing the vehicle with petrol and setting it ablaze.
The attackers subsequently turned on him, inflicting multiple machete wounds to his head, hands and legs, leaving him seriously injured.
Masika was rushed to Reale Hospital in Kitale for emergency treatment before being referred to Eldoret for specialised medical care.
The suspects have been identified as Kennedy Nyongesa Ochieng, who detectives believe was the gang leader, Dan Wakoli Chilungu, Brian Odhiambo Odongo and Hassan Wekesa.
They remain in police custody undergoing processing ahead of their arraignment in court as investigations continue to establish the circumstances surrounding the attack and whether other individuals were involved.
The incident has sparked condemnation from Governor Natembeya, who described the assault as a calculated attempt to intimidate him and his supporters.
Speaking after the incident, Natembeya alleged that the attack was part of a broader pattern of harassment targeting his allies and county officials because of his political position.
He accused the government of orchestrating attacks against people associated with him, claims that have not been independently established.
The governor warned that violence would not force him to abandon his political stand, insisting that those behind the assault must be held accountable.
Masika’s family has also demanded answers, with his brother, Sam Masika, saying they had reported the incident to police and wanted a thorough investigation to establish who was responsible and why his brother was targeted.
The family called for those behind the attack to be brought to justice.
The arrests come amid heightened political tensions in Trans Nzoia, where Natembeya has increasingly positioned himself as a vocal critic of the national government.
However, detectives have not officially established whether the attack was politically motivated or stemmed from personal grievances.
In a statement, the DCI condemned the assault, warning that violence, intimidation and destruction of property should not be used to settle political or personal differences.
The agency said investigators were pursuing all possible leads to identify everyone involved and ensure they face the law.

items.title: Lack of Credit, Equipment Limits Women’s Gains in Agriculture
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Limited access to affordable credit and agricultural equipment is constraining the profitability of women-led agribusinesses in Kenya, despite women farmers generating higher revenue per hectare than their male counterparts.
A nine-year evaluation by the Farm to Market Allia
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Limited access to affordable credit and agricultural equipment is constraining the profitability of women-led agribusinesses in Kenya, despite women farmers generating higher revenue per hectare than their male counterparts.
A nine-year evaluation by the Farm to Market Alliance (FtMA) shows that women smallholders earn an average of Sh82,494 per hectare in main-season revenue, compared to Sh69,833 for men, but the productivity gains are not translating into comparable business profits.
Women-led Farmer Service Centres (FSCs) recorded average annual profits of Sh143,989, significantly lower than the Sh515,253 reported by male-led centers, exposing the financing and equipment challenges facing women entrepreneurs in the agricultural value chain.
The evaluation found that women-led centers own an average of two pieces of equipment, compared to 3.2 for male-led centers, limiting their capacity to provide mechanized services, handle larger volumes of produce and improve post-harvest management.
“The data from our nine-year journey proves beyond doubt that when women and young farmers are connected to reliable inputs, agronomic training, and structured markets, they deliver the highest returns per acre in Kenyan agriculture,” said George Njoroge, FtMA Kenya Country Coordinator.
Access to institutional financing remains another major constraint, with 70 percent of Farmer Service Centres having no formal institutional credit, despite 97 percent maintaining bank accounts.
The report attributes the financing gap partly to agricultural lending requirements that often demand land as collateral, forcing centers to rely on informal borrowing, which accounts for 20 percent of their financing.
The shortage of equipment is also contributing to post-harvest losses, particularly among women farmers.
Only 8.5 percent of Farmer Service Centres across the network own shelling or threshing equipment, with women potentially losing up to half of their bean harvest during manual drying, shelling and bagging.
Market access presents an additional challenge to the commercial growth of smallholder agriculture. Although 88.9 percent of farmers sell their produce, only 3.8 percent have formal off-taker contracts, while just 18.5 percent receive prompt payments.
The findings come as Kenya seeks to strengthen agricultural value chains and improve the commercial viability of smallholder farming, with the evaluation highlighting the need to address financing, post-harvest infrastructure and market access alongside productivity improvements.
The programme, implemented by the Cereal Growers Association since 2017, has expanded from two counties to 13, establishing 2,126 Farmer Service Centres that have reached approximately 401,955 farmers.
The centers have collectively marketed 664,009 metric tonnes of produce, while certified seed adoption among surveyed farmers has reached 88 percent.
Farmers practicing Conservation Agriculture have also recorded a 60 percent increase in main-season maize yields, rising from 2.83 metric tonnes per hectare to 4.53 metric tonnes.
However, the long-term commercial sustainability of the centers remains uncertain, with the evaluation projecting that approximately 70 percent could remain viable after programme support ends.
World Food Programme Kenya Deputy Country Director Bai Mankay Sankoh said the next phase of the programme should focus on building commercially sustainable rural enterprises rather than maintaining centers through donor funding.
“We are not trying to create a permanent network of project-supported centres. We are trying to help build viable rural enterprises that can continue serving farmers because doing so makes commercial sense,” Sankoh said.
The evaluation also identifies young people as an emerging force in agricultural enterprise, with 1,015 youth-run Farmer Service Centres employing an average of 6.1 young people each.
Youth farmers recorded average main-season maize yields of 3.6 metric tonnes per hectare, compared to 2.9 metric tonnes among older farmers, while 91 percent sold their produce into structured markets.
The report calls for targeted asset financing for women-led centers, collateral-free supply-chain credit supported by buyer contracts and improved access to digital agricultural services to address the constraints holding back rural enterprises.

items.title: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
items.summary:
Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But for many, the relief comes with a question: will they be able to return home?
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile
items.text:
Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But for many, the relief comes with a question: will they be able to return home?
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.
Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”
Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.
“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.
On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.
The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.
“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.
Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.
Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched with his community teacher and friends on a laptop. “Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah,” he said. “I did not do anything special. I just sat there and listened, hoping to hear some good news that would give us a peaceful life in the future.”
For Rehan, the first thought was that the verdict could potentially open the door for the Rohingya to return home. “Just imagining that made me so happy,” he said.
The news soon spread through the blocks. Rehan said people were celebrating, while elderly refugees discussed the case and The Gambia’s role in bringing it before the court. The small West African nation was not directly affected by the violence against the Rohingya. Still, it acted as a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, under which all member states have an obligation to prevent and address genocide. In 2022, the court ruled that The Gambia had standing to bring the case.
Rehan’s mother was also delighted when he told her about the ruling. “She was saying that we had won and that we would be able to return to our homeland,” he said.
The celebrations came against a backdrop of difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal, adding to the discomfort of families living in cramped shelters.
It was a reminder that while the verdict had brought recognition to their suffering, it had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a Rohingya youth, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories.
“I was happy, but I was also remembering what happened to us in 2017. I was remembering the horrific military operation, the violence I experienced and the home I had to leave behind,” he said.
Rohingya activist Rohimullah said the announcement was difficult to put into words. It reminded him of those the community had lost and the darkest days of their displacement. He described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope, but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.
Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who researches the Rohingya crisis, said the ICJ ruling was important to ensure justice and accountability from the victims’ perspective.
“In the 21st century, we talk about liberal democracy, globalisation and global justice. Yet such a massive genocide happened before our eyes. The judgement was essential to establish the concept of global justice,” he said.
Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the ruling meant that Dhaka would need stronger assurances from Myanmar about the safe return of Rohingya refugees under any repatriation arrangement.
“I think that this will also have some impact on the dynamics around negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar on the return of Rohingya refugees, now that an international court has said that they experienced genocide,” Kugelman told Al Jazeera.
For the Rohingya, however, the hope of going home remains central. They want accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, the restoration of their rights and citizenship, and a safe and dignified return to Myanmar.
Nurul Amin said he hoped the international community would look beyond the humanitarian crisis and address the political causes of their displacement. He said he wanted freedom in Myanmar, democracy and an end to discrimination and military dictatorship.
“We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more – that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity,” he said.
Maung Solaiman Shah contributed to this story.

items.title: 8 Kenyan students selected for Huawei technology training in China
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Eight Kenyan university students are set to travel to China for specialised training in emerging technologies under Huawei’s 2026 Seeds for the Future programme.
The students were flagged off on Wednesday by the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs ahead of their technic
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Eight Kenyan university students are set to travel to China for specialised training in emerging technologies under Huawei’s 2026 Seeds for the Future programme.
The students were flagged off on Wednesday by the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs ahead of their technical immersion in the Chinese cities of Shenzhen and Dongguan.
Principal Secretary for Foreign Affairs Dr Abraham Korir Sing’Oei, representing Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, presided over the ceremony and handed the Kenyan flag to the delegation.
The fully funded programme will expose the students to practical training at Huawei’s research and development facilities, covering artificial intelligence (AI), 5G and 6G networks, cloud computing and digital power systems.
They will also engage in knowledge exchange with international peers as part of the initiative, which seeks to develop technical skills and nurture local ICT talent.
Sing’Oei said the programme would help bridge the gap between education, market demands and employment opportunities, while strengthening Kenya’s position in the digital economy.
“Education is the pathway for transformation, but only to the extent that we link education to markets, skills, and job creation,” he ssaid.
“By enabling students of technology and leadership in Kenya to travel to Shenzhen and interact directly with a global technology powerhouse like Huawei, we are providing a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Huawei’s investment directly strengthens Nairobi’s position as a digital leader on the African continent.”
The PS said the initiative also builds on commitments made during his official visit to Huawei headquarters in Shenzhen in August 2026.
He noted that the programme aligns with the government’s Digital Superhighway agenda under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA), while reinforcing bilateral relations between Kenya and China.
Speaking on behalf of Huawei Technologies Kenya, Deputy Chief Executive Officer Sun Quan, also known as James, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing local ICT talent.
“This program is named ‘Seeds for the Future.’ As these eight talented students visit Shenzhen to exchange ideas with global technical experts, our hope is that when they return, they will turn into ‘Big Trees’ that contribute significantly to Kenya’s digital economy and national development,” he said.
The ceremony was attended by government and industry representatives, including Deputy Director General for Asia Affairs Ambassador Jane B. Makori, Deputy Director for Higher Education at the State Department for Higher Education Dr Wahome Rureri, and Huawei Technologies’ Khadija Mohamed Ahmed.
Student representative Ahmed Rashid, from the University of Nairobi Faculty of Law, also delivered remarks on behalf of the selected cohort.
Launched globally in 2008, Huawei’s Seeds for the Future programme has engaged nearly 19,800 students from 143 countries and established partnerships with more than 500 universities worldwide, according to the statement.
The 2026 edition forms part of Huawei’s support for Kenya’s digital ecosystem through private-sector infrastructure, public-sector capacity building and technical skills transfer.

items.title: Russell fastest as rain limits running in Las Vegas GP practice
items.summary:
Las Vegas GP: George Russell tops practice for Mercedes as rain limits running on first day of track action
George Russell topped second practice from Pierre Gasly after there was very little running in first practice on a wet first day of track action; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with
items.text:
Las Vegas GP: George Russell tops practice for Mercedes as rain limits running on first day of track action
George Russell topped second practice from Pierre Gasly after there was very little running in first practice on a wet first day of track action; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Friday 20 November 2026 05:42, UK
Mercedes' George Russell topped Practice Two from Alpine's Pierre Gasly as rain limited running on the opening day of track action at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
After no timed laps were completed in first practice due to heavy rain falling throughout, the weather relented to allow plenty of running during the second session, albeit on a damp, slowly drying circuit that prevented the use of slick tyres.
The best lap times came at the end of the session, which took place on Thursday night in Las Vegas, when Russell pipped Gasly by 0.071s, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc three tenths off the pace in third.

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Leclerc and McLaren's Lando Norris, who won last time out in Brazil, had traded the fastest times for most of the session in the wetter conditions.
Norris ended up seventh, behind Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, but the times are likely to matter very little given qualifying and the race are expected to take place in dry conditions.
The schedule in Las Vegas runs a day earlier than a traditional F1 weekend, but the time difference means qualifying will take place at 4am on Saturday morning for UK viewers, with the race following at the same time on Sunday.
Remarkably, there were few incidents and the only red flag across the whole day was for a plastic bag blowing on to the circuit at the high-speed final corner in second practice.
New F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest but will serve a five-place grid penalty after exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation for a second time this season.
Piastri, Williams' Carlos Sainz and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll have 10-place grid penalties for going over various power unit elements, while Haas' Oliver Bearman will start at the back.
Max Verstappen spent most of the day in the garage and completed only 10 laps in total as he finished second practice in 13th.
Verstappen, who is on a run of eight consecutive podiums, felt he had "no power" from the engine on the laps he completed and insisted "it was not normal" despite his engineer suggesting the issue was related to the power unit needing to warm up in the cold condtions.
McLaren and Mercedes have brought upgrades this weekend but the rain on Thursday meant it was virtually impossible to tell whether they made any impact.
Final practice, which gets under way at 12.30am on Saturday for UK viewers, is set to be very busy as the drivers will attempt to get plenty of dry laps in before qualifying.

items.text:
CINCINNATI -- On a night of mixed emotions, Mauricio Pochettino tried to make the moment last as long as possible.
After the final whistle blew, confirming the United States men's national team's 2-0 win over Haiti in the quarterfinals of the Concacaf Nations League, Pochettino was officially no longer the manager of the USMNT. He is now the manager of Manchester United. But he still wanted to savor the moment. He gave hugs to just about everyone in sight: players, coaches, even U.S. Soccer executives JT Batson and Oguchi Onyewu. He took a photo with the entire USMNT staff.
Pochettino completed his requisite postgame news conference, where he said the U.S. players will "achieve big things" in the future. But there was one last team talk to give. That took place in the locker room. There was happiness at the victory. Sadness that Pochettino would no longer take part in the USMNT's journey.
"That was flood works for many people, but it's bound to happen," said U.S. forward Folarin Balogun, referring to the tears that were shed. "We had a really close relationship between his staff and us as players. I think he was really connected."
U.S. captain Tyler Adams said Pochettino had to "calm himself when it got too emotional."
As send-offs go, Tuesday's win over Haiti was about as good as could be expected for Pochettino's last game in charge. Given that the U.S. carried a six-goal cushion into the match from the first leg, it was a game for managing the result as well as the emotions. Sure, the U.S. wasn't quite as clinical in front of goal in this match as it was in the first leg, but the goals the team did score were of high quality. Christian Pulisic scored on a bicycle kick from Weston McKennie's cross in the 25th minute, and Julian Hall doubled the lead just before halftime, deftly taking McKennie's lofted pass and then lifting his shot just over Alexandre Pierre in the Haiti goal. The result made for an 8-0 victory for the U.S. on aggregate.
At which point the long goodbye that had lasted for the past 10 days accelerated. Pochettino's nickname during his playing days was "The Sheriff," given the way he commanded his team's back line as a central defender. On Tuesday, his role of sheriff was more cinematic in nature, making like one of those lawmen in a Hollywood Western. In his view, his work was done. It was time to move on to the next stop to revive a team's fortunes, in this case Manchester United.
It's an exit like no other manager in U.S. men's national team history has experienced. None of his full-time predecessors, at least in the modern era, left of their own accord. Some, such as Bora Milutinovic and Bruce Arena (version 1.0), were nudged aside. Others, such as Steve Sampson, Jurgen Klinsmann and Arena (version 2.0), were shoved out the door.
Not so for Pochettino. Hence the mixed emotions. The Argentine was largely given a hero's send-off Tuesday. After the match, fans chanted "Poch-e-tti-no." "Take Me Home, Country Roads" blared over the loudspeakers one last time. Pochettino soaked in the adulation, applauding the fans. Yet all of this was happening in spite of the fact that he's leaving less than three months after signing a new contract with U.S. Soccer. At the least, there has been an acknowledgment that departing for a higher-profile job is how things work at the highest levels of the sport. There are only so many coaching jobs at the same level as Manchester United. It still makes for an odd dynamic, though it's one the players accept.
"That's football, and that's the world of football," said midfielder Weston McKennie about Pochettino's departure prior to Tuesday's match. "You say goodbyes, and new people come in, and you get used to it after playing a long time in this type of level."
Some emotions have more clarity. Pochettino has projected a vibe these past 10 days of a man torn in two, conflicted between a job with U.S. Soccer that he enjoyed, and that of Manchester United, one he has wanted for much of his managerial career. The reality isn't as muddled. Certainly, Pochettino is appreciative of how he was treated by U.S. Soccer throughout his USMNT tenure, especially after his experience at Chelsea fell short of his expectations. He was treated with honesty and respect, and more critically, allowed to get on with the work of constructing a team for the FIFA World Cup. He also created a genuine bond with the players. That was very real.
But make no mistake, Pochettino didn't have to think twice about taking the Manchester United job. Being sensitive to the feelings of his bosses at U.S. Soccer, and having fond memories of being in charge of the USMNT -- and even shedding a tear or two -- is not the same thing as having to make an agonizing decision. The negotiations were done and dusted inside of a week. Following Saturday's 6-0 blowout of Haiti in the first leg, half of Pochettino's staff, including top assistant Jesus Perez, departed for Manchester to get on with the business of starting their new adventure.
The lack of internal conflict was also made clear during a roundtable with reporters on Monday. This is a man very much looking forward to the future with excitement. There will be no looking back.
"It's true that when I arrive at this type of possibility, like United, you say, 'Yes, I want that,'" he said. "I want to prove again myself."
Yet the mixed emotions were there until the very end. The last person Pochettino hugged postmatch was none other than Pulisic. The two have certainly endured some ups and downs in their relationship during Pochettino's tenure with the USMNT. Viewed from the outside, there was professionalism, but little warmth. Perhaps that began to thaw a little at the very end. The team-first ethos of Pochettino had imprinted itself on Pulisic.

items.text:
At the risk of stating the obvious, it's tough to earn a call-up for a national team.
For the United States men, who have seen a rise in players moving to more competitive leagues in Europe, this is no different. Long gone are the days in which simply playing in the Premier League or representing a UEFA Champions League-level club is enough to guarantee a national team spot.
More depth and talented options are clearly a positive for the U.S, but that also means that the number of high-profile players who may not get an opportunity on the international stage has also increased. Whether it be due to a player's skill or simply not fitting into a manager's vision, there are a handful of established players who found minutes under Mauricio Pochettino hard to come by.
But with Pochettino now on the ground at Manchester United, the outlook for the national team squad has been reset. With a yet-to-be-named replacement on the horizon, who are the players who could benefit the most in a new era for the USMNT?
Aidan Morris | 25 | Midfielder | Middlesbrough
Games: 7 (tied for 32nd most in Pochettino era)
Consistent minutes for an English Championship side that nearly got promoted to the Premier League? Check. Previous domestic success as an MLS All-Star and two-time MLS Cup champion? Check. Praise in Europe from well-respected coaches? Check.
A key role for the USMNT? Apparently not.
This perhaps says more about a crowded pool of midfielders for the U.S., but Morris claimed just one appearance for Pochettino this year during a March friendly against Portugal. Since then, he's been on the outside looking in, but if he continues to show off his traits as a well-rounded central midfielder, the next coach may be willing to give him more opportunities.
Still just 25, he could be at the peak of his abilities by the time the 2028 Copa América and 2030 FIFA World Cup roll around.
Yunus Musah | 23 | Midfielder | AC Milan
Games: 9 (T-28th most in Pochettino era)
Musah's 2026 World Cup fate appeared cemented as soon as he decided to take a break from the 2025 Gold Cup, due to fatigue. Coupled with sporadic minutes in Serie A on loan with Atalanta, Musah was not only absent from the World Cup roster, but went more than 18 months without a national team call-up between March 2025 and September 2026.
The good news is that he's still just 23 years old, and in a more prominent role under Ruben Amorim that has provided much-needed minutes, the versatile midfielder has once again showcased that he can play in a handful of different positions.
And don't forget: Even though he missed out on 2026's edition, Musah was one of the USMNT's breakout stars of the 2022 World Cup.
Joe Scally | 23 | Defender | Borussia Mönchengladbach
Games: 13 (T-19th most in Pochettino era)
To be fair, of the five players on this list, Scally did go to the 2026 World Cup. In fact, the fullback earned a start in one group stage game.
Nonetheless, for an American who is a consistent starter in the Bundlesliga, it's probably a letdown to be typically third choice in the right-back depth chart. Alex Freeman is the clear favorite as the starter in that spot, but could the next coach begin to favor backup minutes for a more defensive-minded and adaptable defender like Scally?
He's been linked to bigger clubs in the past, and if he moves to a more noteworthy side, that could make things interesting in the fight for minutes across the back line.
Johnny Cardoso | 25 | Midfielder | Atlético Madrid
Games: 6 (T-35th in Pochettino era)
On paper, Cardoso should be a USMNT star. He's well-versed in the Champions League and plays for a genuine powerhouse in global soccer that is Atlético Madrid.
There are two problems, though. One, he has missed 19 games through injury since making the move to the Spanish capital in July 2025, making it hard for him to demonstrate any form or fitness at club level -- including suffering a May ankle injury that ruled him out of the World Cup. And two, when he has been fit enough to feature for the national team, he's been prone to costly errors that are completely antithetical to what he has shown in LaLiga.
Now fit after resuming play in August, it's only a matter of time before the next USMNT coach attempts their own roll of the dice when it comes to finding a place for the defensive midfielder.
Tanner Tessmann | 25 | Midfielder | Lyon
Games: 12 (T-22nd most in Pochettino era)
There are some similarities between Tessmann and Cardoso. Both, on paper, had the résumé to shine with the USMNT, but looked more like a square peg in a round hole.
Twelve appearances are still a decent number, but his omission from Pochettino's World Cup roster was a surprise. Although he had suffered a muscle injury before the tournament, the expectation was that he would be fit by the start of the World Cup.
Aggressive, but also possessing the ability to provide accurate distribution and the occasional shot from distance, Tessmann could be back in the mix soon.

by returning `-1` for invalid inputs. It also provides a similar guard
for `EVP_DecodeBlock()`, and fixes the incorrect length check in the
`base64encode()` function of `http_client.c`. Also updates the
documentation and adds new tests.

items.title: Socceroos’ future looks bright as Australia stun Argentina in U17 World Cup
items.summary:
Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon has demonstrated why he’s one of the most exciting talents in Australian football, leading the Joeys to a shock 2-0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style.

items.text:
Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon has demonstrated why he’s one of the most exciting talents in Australian football, leading the Joeys to a shock 2-0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style.
The brilliant young winger had his shot deflected for an own goal on the hour and then produced an audaciously cheeky finish 11 minutes later to seal the opening-day win on Friday (AEDT) as Carl Veart’s side announced their return to the global boys’ competition for the first time in seven years.
Against one of the powerhouse football nations, Australia had their backs to the wall, having to make 31 clearances as Argentina enjoyed two-thirds of the possession and 22 shots on goal. But the Joeys fought back after the break, spearheaded by Akon, who hailed their second-half heist as “amazing”.
The 17-year-old livewire provided the real star quality, and it was soon evident why the Sky Blues had wanted to keep him in Australia for their A-League Men campaign instead of releasing him for the tournament; a decision that triggered widespread backlash before being reversed.
Akon caused havoc from the start down the right flank, his neat through ball in the fifth minute almost resulting in a goal for Central Coast Mariners’ Luke Becvinovski.
The teenage sensation then struck after the break following another dangerous foray down the right that ended with his shot across goal deflecting off the hapless Alvaro Guich and into the net.
In the 71st minute, Mariners midfielder Oli O’Carroll expertly picked off an Argentina attack before Brisbane’s Emmett Shaw released Akon with a slide-rule left-foot pass, the winger going on to dummy the goalkeeper before slotting into an empty net.
It only got worse for Argentina when substitute Benjamin Vallejos got sent off for a reckless challenge in stoppage time.
But it wasn’t all about Akon, a considerable talent who’s already made his national U23 bow. At the other end, Charlie Wilson-Papps, the young goalkeeper who’s on the books at Brighton and Hove Albion, made half-a-dozen fine saves and kept a clean sheet.
“I do it for my teammates, I do it for my family at home, so to make them proud is is the most important thing,” said Akon as he clutched the player-of-the-match trophy afterwards.
Akon’s only worry came with the video checking of his goal. “Ah, that was nerve-racking, man,” he said. “Because at 1-0, it was a very scary game. So to be able to seal it like that, the coach was telling me it was a goal.
“The first goal? It wasn’t really my goal, but I just wanted to do the Tim Cahill, start off the tournament like that. So, yeah, the knee side had to come with it.
“Now, the group, we’re really confident, really confident in our ability, and I think that showed today.”
Next up on Sunday for the Joeys will be Denmark, who lost 4-0 to Mozambique in their Group C opener on Thursday.

items.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
items.summary:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering
items.text:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”
“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.
Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

items.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
items.summary:
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
- Published
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaf
items.text:
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
- Published
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
- 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted 
  - Published11 November
- A really simple guide to climate change 
  - Published6 November
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.

items.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
items.summary:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.
At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocke
items.text:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.
At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.
Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.
However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”
With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.
$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.
Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.
Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.
28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.
The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.
More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.
Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.
All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.summary: After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those
items.text:
After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. Simon Burnton
Positivity surrounds Aston Villa despite them failing to win in four matches, the last of which ended in agonising fashion; they had to settle for a 4-4 draw at Manchester United after twice squandering a two-goal advantage. Villa should have managed the final minutes better, but a home date with Sunderland presents an opportunity to return to winning ways. Unai Emery needs to eliminate the defensive naivety that has blighted some performances and the expected absence of Matty Cash, this time owing to concussion sustained on Poland duty, would deny the Villa manager his preferred defensive lineup. This fixture threw up a classic last season, Tammy Abraham scoring a stoppage-time winner to extend the visitors’ miserable record at Villa Park. Sunderland have won on only two of their past 17 league visits, their last victory coming in 2011 courtesy of the former Villa loanee Phil Bardsley. Ben Fisher
The last time Alex Scott played for Bournemouth, Marco Rose was yet to taste victory in the Premier League. When the 23-year-old returns to midfield he will do so with the team in a totally different place. Bournemouth have racked up eight straight wins in all competitions before hosting Nottingham Forest on Saturday and Scott, who has been able to build his fitness during the international break after a thigh problem, may have to wait his turn owing to the form of Tyler Adams and Ryan Christie. If Rose opts for momentum, then Eli Junior Kroupi, fresh from scoring his first France goal, could make his first start of the season after sustaining a freak foot injury in pre-season. Bournemouth have hardly been short of firepower, though, with Evanilson scoring seven goals in his past eight games. BF
Chelsea left Wearside battered and bruised after being pushed around by Brian Brobbey. The Sunderland forward bullied Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill, who had to be substituted at half-time, and won the game’s decisive penalty with a solo run that left Xabi Alonso angry with his side’s powderpuff defending. Alonso insisted Chelsea had prepared for Brobbey’s threat; the Chelsea manager will hope they are better at putting the plan into practice when they face another target man on Saturday. Leeds head to Stamford Bridge and will look to Dominic Calvert-Lewin, fresh from helping England get over the line against Spain last weekend, to unnerve Alonso’s defenders. Jacob Steinberg
Thomas Frank’s first assessment of his new charges after taking over at Crystal Palace this week included the nuggets that “we’re conceding too many goals … we need to work on the defensive side of things with principles, attitude, everything regarding that”, and in particular “we need to work on the set pieces, that’s key”. If he can’t inspire an immediate improvement this is where this match could be decided, being as it is an encounter between the league’s worst set-piece defenders – no one comes close to the 67 shots and xG of 7.44 coughed up by Palace at restarts – and the best. Though Coventry have let in one goal from set pieces, and neither Brentford nor Liverpool have shipped any, the hosts’ set-piece xG of 1.65 is a league low, and they were equally outstanding from dead-ball situations in the Championship last season. The home side will be boosted by the return of the 6ft 4in defender Bobby Thomas, who, despite a calf injury that meant he missed the last two games and the final third of the one before that, has still made more clearances than any other Coventry player. SB
It may have been a slightly strange week for Tottenham fans. They have watched as their former managers Mauricio Pochettino and Thomas Frank have been installed at Manchester United and Crystal Palace respectively, while their current head coach, Roberto De Zerbi, picked up the Premier League’s manager of the month award for October. That is reflective of the improvement De Zerbi has overseen in recent weeks, with Spurs happy to move forward with the Italian and avoid the chaos enveloping some of their rivals. The long-held assumption among some connected to Tottenham that Pochettino would one day return to save the club must now be banished; De Zerbi needs full buy-in from everyone to build his project. That’s the only way Spurs can ensure they steer clear of future crises. Dominic Booth
With the temperature in Newcastle forecast to dip to 0C at kick-off, Matthias Jaissle is perhaps hoping that his team’s guests from north London (where a balmy 9C is predicted at 5.30pm) freeze in the Tyneside chill. Otherwise it is hard to envisage his young side overcoming a formidable looking Arsenal on a day when Newcastle’s head coach seeks what would be only his second win in seven games. Home fans will not merely be hurt by the sight of their much-missed former captain Bruno Guimarães wearing Arsenal colours but decidedly nervous about a fixture that precedes a run of tricky engagements involving a trip to Brighton and home dates with Manchester United and Sunderland. items.title: Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level
items.summary:
Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level
- Published
It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.
That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across t
items.text:
Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level
- Published
It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.
That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.
In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.
Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.
On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.
One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.
Lyon superior in every department
Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.
In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.
Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.
Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.
Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.
"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers said.
"They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances."
Lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.
Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.
Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.
As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.
Slegers also said Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.
Asked how far off Lyon they currently are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.
"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.
"But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us."
Williamson 'aware of where the gaps are'
Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.
They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.
"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.
"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period."
It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.
Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.
They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.
Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.
Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.
Giraldez said time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.
"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.
"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.
"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season."

items.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
items.summary: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic
items.text:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

items.title: England get one-match suspended ban on away tickets for anti-pope chants in Spain
items.summary:
England have been handed a suspended one-match ban on away ticket sales by Uefa in relation to “racist and/or discriminatory” behaviour by fans at Sunday’s 3-2 Nations League victory over Spain. The punishment is suspended for two years.
Uefa has also fined the Football Association €15,000 (£12,500)
items.text:
England have been handed a suspended one-match ban on away ticket sales by Uefa in relation to “racist and/or discriminatory” behaviour by fans at Sunday’s 3-2 Nations League victory over Spain. The punishment is suspended for two years.
Uefa has also fined the Football Association €15,000 (£12,500), with the behaviour in question believed to be the chant of “Fuck the pope and the IRA” at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid. A further charge in the next two years could trigger a ban on away fans for a competitive game.
In a statement given to the Mail, the FA said: “We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police who attend all England home and away matches to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action.”
Uefa’s control, ethics and disciplinary body announced that it had decided “to fine the English Football Association €15,000 and to order against the English Football Association a full restriction on selling tickets to its supporters for one representative team competition away match, for the racist and/or discriminatory behaviour of its supporters.
“Said full restriction on selling tickets to supporters for one away match is suspended for a probationary period of two years, starting from the date of the present decision.”
The relevant article of Uefa’s disciplinary regulations reads: “If one or more of a member association or club’s supporters engage in the behaviour described in paragraph 1 [insulting the human dignity of a person or group of persons on whatever grounds, including skin colour, race, religion, ethnic origin, gender or sexual orientation], the member association or club responsible incurs a minimum of a fine and either a partial stadium closure or a restriction on selling tickets to its supporters for away matches.”
The match had been preceded by Thomas Tuchel reminding his players of the anti-racism protocols, given the last match between the sides in Madrid, in 2004, had notoriously been marred by abuse aimed at England’s black players.
Last month Spain were fined £15,000 and ordered to play their next friendly with a partial stadium closure after discriminatory chants about Muslims during March’s match against Egypt in Barcelona.
Sunday’s chant is a staple for some England fans but sung relatively rarely in stadiums. Several more frequently heard chants target only the IRA, including inserting “No surrender” into the national anthem.

items.title: OL Lyonnes show their class to hit Arsenal’s ambitions for a top-four WCL finish
items.summary:
Arsenal’s hopes of earning automatic progression to the Champions League quarter-finals were dashed by OL Lyonnes, as the French side continued their statement form in Europe.
Goals in either half from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay were the difference at Meadow Park and Lyonnes are top of the tabl
items.text:
Arsenal’s hopes of earning automatic progression to the Champions League quarter-finals were dashed by OL Lyonnes, as the French side continued their statement form in Europe.
Goals in either half from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay were the difference at Meadow Park and Lyonnes are top of the table and still yet to concede in the league phase with one game remaining.
It feels like Lyonnes are playing with a fire and intensity fueled by their loss to Barcelona in May’s Champions League final. They look a more formidable, coherent and hungry side, on a mission to end a four-year run without lifting the trophy they won eight times in a 12-year period between 2011 and 2022.
The visit of the eight-time European champions was always going to be challenging for the Gunners and based on current form getting a result would be even tougher. Last season’s runners-up had scored 20 goals without conceding in their first four Champions League matches prior to their trip to Borehamwood and they have scored 49 in their nine Première Ligue games.
The lack of competitiveness in the France top flight also means they were able to rotate heavily at the weekend between their two European games. Jonatan Giráldez made 11 changes for their 1-0 defeat of Saint-Malo on Saturday before returning to his first-choice lineup against the 2025 Champions League winners.
Arsenal were not afforded the luxury of an easy league match after their battling 1-1 draw against Barcelona last week, playing a critical and tricky game with London City Lionesses, which also ended 1-1. Renée Slegers made two changes to the team that hosted ambitious London City, with Ona Batlle having picked up a knock Taylor Hinds played at left-back and Kyra Cooney-Cross started ahead of Kim Little.
They had their backs against the wall at a bitterly cold Meadow Park, as Giráldez’s Galacticos controlled the game. The away team had almost 69% possession in the first half and amassed 12 shots to Arsenal’s one.
The surprise was that Lyonnes weren’t further ahead at the break, with Brand’s 24th-minute goal the difference, the full-back sweeping in Vicki Bècho’s ball in from the right.
Brand was back to haunt the Gunners, having scored in both legs of last season’s semi-final between the two teams, with the French side progressing to face Barcelona in the final with a 4-3 aggregate win.
Arsenal were better after the break, but Lyonnes soaked up a brief spell of Arsenal pressure, Marie-Antoinette Katoto the only player left forward as they banked back and crowded the box to give the home players few options.
They increased their margin and dampened the mood soon after, Tabitha Chawinga’s cross from the left was collected by Katoto and the France forward laid it off for Dumornay who took a touch before powering the ball into the roof of the net.
It was an emphatic and unstoppable finish from one of the best players in the world as a mist lowered over Meadow Park.
It was a testament to the relationship between the club and the fans that the crowd remained in full voice, they urged the players in red and white forward, the North Bank doing all it could to lift the spirits of their struggling side.
There were no more goals and Arsenal’s single shot on target was almost the last kick of the game as a controlled Lyonnes performance demonstrated the gulf in quality between the sides.
Arsenal need to quickly move on, with West Ham their last game before the international break. They had needed a win to have any serious chance of earning a place in top four, avoiding a quarter-final playoff place.
They now sit eighth and will face Inter in their final league phase match in December, with the Italian side needing a win against the north London team to keep any hopes of a playoff place alive. That will not be easy, but a seeded playoff place is in their hands, if they want it.

items.title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
items.summary:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.
A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.
By T
items.text:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.
A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.
By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.
Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.
“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”
But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.
The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.
It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.
On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”
Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.
The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.
Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.
The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.
Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.
On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.
